# SEVerA: Verified Self-Evolving Agents

CCS: LLM Agents Automated Verification

Debangshu Banerjee Note: These authors contributed equally to this work.
email: <db21@illinois.edu> Affiliation: University of Illinois
Urbana-Champaign, USA , Changming Xu email: <cx23@illinois.edu>
Affiliation: University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign, USA , Eugene Ie
email: <eugeneie@google.com> Affiliation: Google, USA , Ming Zhang
email: <mingzhang@google.com> Affiliation: Google, USA , Daiyi Peng
email: <daiyip@google.com> Affiliation: Google, USA , Chu-Cheng Lin
email: <kitsing@google.com> Affiliation: Google, USA and Gagandeep Singh

###### Abstract.

Recent advances have demonstrated the effectiveness of self-evolving LLM
agents on tasks such as program repair and scientific discovery. In this
paradigm, a planner LLM synthesizes an agent program that invokes
parametric models, including probabilistic generative models such as
LLMs, smaller neural networks, and external tools such as SMT solvers.
These components are then tuned per task to improve performance.
However, unlike traditional constraint-guided program synthesis,
existing self-evolving agent frameworks provide no formal guarantees of
safety or correctness. Because such synthesized programs are often
executed autonomously on unseen inputs, the lack of formal guarantees
raises serious reliability and security concerns. To address this gap,
we formulate agentic code generation as a constrained learning problem
that combines hard formal specifications with soft objectives capturing
task utility. We introduce Formally Guarded Generative Models (FGGM),
which allow the planner LLM to specify a formal output contract for each
generative-model call using first-order logic. Each FGGM call
automatically wraps the underlying parametric generative model in a
rejection sampler with a verified fallback, treating model outputs as
samples from a proposal distribution. As a result, every returned output
satisfies the specified contract for any input and any parameter setting
of the underlying model. Building on FGGM, we present SEVerA
(*S*elf-*E*volving Verified *A*gents), a three-stage framework for
solving constrained learning problems arising from agent synthesis. In
_Search_, the planner LLM synthesizes candidate parametric programs that
may contain multiple FGGM calls. In _Verification_, we prove correctness
with respect to the hard constraints for all parameter values, reducing
the problem to unconstrained learning. In _Learning_, we apply scalable
gradient-based optimization, including GRPO-style fine-tuning for LLMs,
to improve the soft objective while preserving formal correctness. We
evaluate SEVerA on constrained symbolic regression, invariant generation
for Dafny programs, symbolic mathematical expression synthesis, and
policy-compliant agentic tool use ($`\tau^{2}`$-bench). Across all
tasks, SEVerA achieves zero constraint violations while simultaneously
improving task performance over unconstrained and state-of-the-art
baselines. Our results demonstrate that formal behavioral constraints
not only guarantee correctness but also prune the space of candidate
programs, steering synthesis toward higher-quality agents.

###### Keywords: 

LLM Agents, Automated Verification, Deductive Program Synthesis.

## 1. Introduction

Recent works have leveraged the code-generation capabilities of large
language models (LLMs) to automatically synthesize LLM-based agents,
expressed as programs, from natural language task descriptions ([Wang et
al., 2024](#bib.bib1); [Wang et al., 2023](#bib.bib2); [Hu et al.,
2025](#bib.bib3); [Zhuge et al., 2024](#bib.bib5); [Gao et al.,
2025](#bib.bib6)). Given a user-defined task, a planner LLM generates a
program that invokes parametric models, including LLMs, smaller neural
networks, and external tools such as SMT solvers, and executes this
program on user inputs to compute outputs. While this paradigm is
powerful, it introduces serious safety and reliability concerns: the
synthesized programs are executed autonomously on unseen inputs. Modern
self-evolving frameworks ([Zhou et al., 2024](#bib.bib7); [Fang et al.,
2025](#bib.bib8); [Wang et al., 2026](#bib.bib9); [Tian et al.,
2025](#bib.bib10)) further complicate formal safety verification as they
fine-tune the parameters of models embedded in the synthesized programs
to improve task-specific performance. Consequently, any correctness
guarantee provided on an agentic program must continue to hold after
parameter updates.

The absence of formal safety verification leads to failures across
diverse domains. In program verification, agents cheat by subtly
modifying the input program (e.g., altering variable initializations) so
that the modified program with proposed annotations passes verification,
inflating task accuracy ([Banerjee et al., 2026](#bib.bib44)). In code
repair, agents delete failing tests rather than fixing the underlying
bugs ([Zhong et al., 2025](#bib.bib48)). In agentic tool use,
unconstrained agents violate domain-specific policies, such as refund
eligibility and booking-modification rules, on 65-76% of interactions
([Kamath et al., 2025](#bib.bib29)). In deployment, rogue agents have
been observed bypassing security protections in the wild ([Guo et al.,
2024](#bib.bib11); [Lee et al., 2025](#bib.bib12); [Guardian,
2026](#bib.bib13)). These are not isolated incidents; they are a
consequence of evaluating synthesized agents solely on soft performance
metrics without formal behavioral specifications. Natural-language task
descriptions and testing on fixed inputs is not sufficient to completely
prevent such failures. Agentic programs need formal hard constraints to
ensure safety. In this paper, we aim to achieve both the formal
guarantees of constraint-guided synthesis ([Alur et al.,
2013](#bib.bib14)) and the flexibility and performance benefits of
self-evolving agentic frameworks.

Key Challenges: We summarize the challenges below.

- •
  Balancing Safety and Performance: A safe agent synthesis algorithm
  must ensure formal correctness guarantees while simultaneously
  improving task-specific performance. Existing work on deductive
  program synthesis ([Alur et al., 2013](#bib.bib14); [Kim et al.,
  2021](#bib.bib18); [Solar-Lezama, 2013](#bib.bib20)) provides formal
  guarantees but typically does not optimize task-specific performance
  objectives. Meanwhile, popular gradient-based optimization methods for
  LLMs, such as GRPO ([Shao et al., 2024](#bib.bib22)), empirically
  improve output quality but provide no assurance that post-training
  outputs satisfy specified constraints.
- •
  Enforcing Constraints per Model Call: Generative models (GMs), such as
  LLMs, may be used in an agentic program at different places with
  different constraints. For example, one call may require generating
  Python programs, while another may require producing symbolic
  mathematical expressions conforming to a specific formal grammar.
  Thus, we require a mechanism to specify formal output constraints for
  each GM call in an agentic program and a way to use these
  specifications to verify that an agentic program satisfies the
  user-provided behavioral specification. Recent work on constrained
  decoding ([Ugare et al., 2025b](#bib.bib24); [Park et al.,
  2024](#bib.bib25); [Banerjee et al., 2025](#bib.bib45)) can enforce
  context-free grammar–based syntactic constraints and limited semantic
  constraints such as variable naming or simple type checks. However,
  these approaches are restricted in the types of constraints they
  support and require modifying the model’s decoding procedure, which
  limits their applicability to open-source models. Moreover,
  constrained decoding strategies are known to distort the output
  distribution, producing outputs that satisfy constraints but degrade
  task performance ([Park et al., 2024](#bib.bib25); [Banerjee et al.,
  2025](#bib.bib45)).

Our Contributions: We summarize our contributions below.

- •
  We introduce the novel concept of Formally Guarded Generative Models
  (FGGM), which allow us to define and enforce local contracts on model
  calls through formal input-output specifications expressed in
  first-order logic. FGGM operates solely on LLM output strings and can
  be applied to both open and closed source models. Using FGGM, we
  retain the formal guarantees of deductive synthesis while utilizing
  the performance gained through gradient-based parameter optimization.
- •
  We introduce SEVerA: the first self-evolving agent synthesis algorithm
  with verifiable guarantees. The approach consists of three stages: (a)
  _Search_, where a planner LLM samples program strings in a
  verifier-aware language such as Dafny, and use the proposed FGGMs to
  establish local contracts on the embedded model calls; (b) _Verify_,
  where the language’s built-in verifier is used to prove that the
  sampled programs satisfy all specified contracts over all parameters
  of the embedded parametric model calls; and (c) _Learn_, where
  verified parametric programs reduce the constrained learning problem
  to an unconstrained optimization problem over model parameters,
  enabling scalable gradient-based training without sacrificing
  correctness.
- •
  We prove that SEVerA is _sound_: any agent returned satisfies the
  behavioral specification for all inputs and all parameter values
  (Theorem [5.4](#S5.Thmtheorem4 "Theorem 5.4 (Soundness). ‣ 5.3. Theoretical Results ‣ 5. Technical Details ‣ SEVerA: Verified Self-Evolving Agents")).
  We also establish a _sufficient condition_ under which a verified
  agent exists that satisfies the hard constraints while incurring no
  greater task loss than any unconstrained generative model with initial
  parameters, with strict improvement whenever the unconstrained model
  violates the specification
  (Theorem [5.5](#S5.Thmtheorem5 "Theorem 5.5 (Sufficient Success Condition). ‣ 5.3. Theoretical Results ‣ 5. Technical Details ‣ SEVerA: Verified Self-Evolving Agents")).
- •
  We evaluate SEVerA on tasks spanning LLM-assisted program
  verification, symbolic math synthesis, agentic tool use, and
  constrained symbolic regression. Across all benchmarks, SEVerA
  achieves provably zero constraint violations while outperforming
  state-of-the-art agents in task performance: 97.0% verification rate
  on HumanEvalDafny (vs. 86.9% for the best baseline), 66.0% accuracy on
  GSM-Symbolic (vs. 44.7% for the best constrained-decoding method), and
  52.6% pass rate $`\tau^{2}`$-bench’s airline domain using Qwen3-8B.
  Notably, on $`\tau^{2}`$-bench airline SEVerA even beats Agent-C
  ([Kamath et al., 2025](#bib.bib29)) with Claude Sonnet 4.5, a
  state-of-the-art constrained agent using a frontier model. These
  results demonstrate that behavioral constraints do not merely enforce
  safety but actively prune the search space of candidate programs and
  steer synthesis toward higher-quality agents. The code is available on
  [github](https://github.com/uiuc-focal-lab/severa).

## 2. Background

Notations and Terminology: We use $`\Sigma`$ to denote the alphabet, a
finite set of characters. All LLMs output finite strings over
$`\Sigma`$. We use lowercase letters $`(x)`$ to denote constants, bold
letters $`(\boldsymbol{x})`$ to denote strings, capital letters $`(X)`$
to denote sets (including sets of functions), and $`|\boldsymbol{x}|`$
to denote string length. In the rest of the paper, we treat neural
networks as a restricted form of generative model that produces a single
output for a fixed input.

LLMs: LLMs $`\mathcal{L}:\Sigma^{*}\to\Sigma^{*}`$ are probabilistic
string generators that, given a prompt $`\boldsymbol{p}\in\Sigma^{*}`$
over the alphabet $`\Sigma`$, sample an output string
$`\boldsymbol{y}\in\Sigma^{*}`$. Typically, the output length
$`|\boldsymbol{y}|`$ is bounded by a fixed user-specified $`n`$, i.e.,
$`|\boldsymbol{y}|\leq n`$ or equivalently
$`\boldsymbol{y}\in\Sigma^{\leq n}`$. Fixed-length generation
$`\mathcal{L}_{n}:\Sigma^{*}\to\Sigma^{\leq n}`$ is implemented by
iteratively composing two high-level steps, repeated at most $`n`$
times. Each iteration samples a single character (sometimes referred to
as a token) from $`\Sigma`$ or the special end-of-sequence symbol
$`\langle eos\rangle\notin\Sigma{}`$ that marks termination of
generation. The first step is the distribution prediction step, defined
as
$`\mathcal{L}^{p}:\Sigma^{*}\to\mathcal{P}({\Sigma\cup\langle eos\rangle})`$,
which maps a prefix string $`\boldsymbol{x}\in\Sigma^{*}`$ to a
probability distribution over $`\Sigma\cup\langle eos\rangle`$. This
distribution captures how likely each character is to appear next. The
second step is the decoding step, defined as
$`\mathcal{D}:\Sigma^{*}\times\mathcal{P}({\Sigma\cup\langle eos\rangle})\to\Sigma\cup\langle eos\rangle`$,
which draws the next character using the current prefix
$`\boldsymbol{x}`$ and the predicted distribution. If the decoding step
produces $`\langle eos\rangle`$, the generation terminates. Otherwise,
the sampled character $`c`$ is appended to the prefix, and generation
continues. Henceforth, we drop the subscript $`n`$ for simplicity.

###### Definition 2.1 (LLMs).

For a fixed $`n\in\mathbb{N}`$, an LLM is a bounded string generator
$`\mathcal{L}_{n}:\Sigma^{*}\to\Sigma^{\leq n}`$ that samples an output
string $`\boldsymbol{y}\in\Sigma^{\leq n}`$ for input
$`\boldsymbol{x}`$. $`\boldsymbol{y}`$ on $`\boldsymbol{x}`$ is computed
recursively as $`\boldsymbol{y}_{0}=\boldsymbol{x}`$, and
$`\boldsymbol{y}_{i}=\boldsymbol{y}_{i-1}\cdot c_{i}`$ if
($`\forall j\leq i.c_{j}\neq\langle eos\rangle)`$ else
$`\boldsymbol{y}_{i-1}`$ where $`i\in[n]`$,
$`c_{i}=\mathcal{D}(\boldsymbol{y}_{i-1},\mathcal{L}^{p}(\boldsymbol{y}_{i-1}))`$
and $`\boldsymbol{x}\cdot\boldsymbol{y}=\boldsymbol{y}_{n}`$.

Rejection Sampling: Rejection sampling is a popular Monte Carlo method
for generating samples from a _target distribution_ $`\pi_{t}`$ when
direct sampling from $`\pi_{t}`$ is difficult. Instead, it relies on a
_proposal distribution_ $`\pi_{p}`$ from which sampling is easy. The
support set $`S(\pi_{p})`$ (see
Definition [2.2](#S2.Thmtheorem2 "Definition 2.2. ‣ 2. Background ‣ SEVerA: Verified Self-Evolving Agents"))
must cover $`S(\pi_{t})`$, i.e., $`S(\pi_{t})\subseteq S(\pi_{p})`$.
Intuitively, $`\pi_{p}`$ generates candidate samples, and the rejection
sampler decides whether to accept each candidate, rejecting those that
are unlikely under $`\pi_{t}`$ (details in
Appendix [B](#A2 "Appendix B Rejection Sampling Details ‣ SEVerA: Verified Self-Evolving Agents")).
The rejection sampler guarantees that no accepted sample lies outside
$`S(\pi_{t})`$.

###### Definition 2.2.

Let $`\pi`$ be a probability distribution over $`\Omega`$ with density
function $`D_{\pi}:\Omega\to\mathbb{R}^{+}`$. The support set $`S(\pi)`$
of $`\pi`$ captures all points with positive probability
$`S(\pi)=\{x\in\Omega;|D_{\pi}(x)>0\}`$.

Self-evolving LLM agents: In this work, we focus on LLM agents modeled
as programs $`f:T_{i}\to T_{o}`$ that, given any user input
$`x\in T_{i}`$, compute the output $`y=f(x)`$. Typically, $`f`$ is
written in a popular imperative language such as Python. The program
invokes one or more parametric models (formally defined in
§ [5.1](#S5.SS1 "5.1. Search Space ‣ 5. Technical Details ‣ SEVerA: Verified Self-Evolving Agents")),
such as LLMs, as well as other tools such as an SMT solver, to compute
the output $`y`$. All parametric models $`\mathcal{F}_{p}`$ and tool
calls $`\mathcal{F}_{c}`$ are provided as a collection of
pre-implemented library functions. We denote this library by
$`\mathcal{F}=\mathcal{F}_{p}\cup\mathcal{F}_{c}`$ (formal definition in
§ [5.1](#S5.SS1 "5.1. Search Space ‣ 5. Technical Details ‣ SEVerA: Verified Self-Evolving Agents")).
In the self-evolving paradigm, the program $`f`$ is not handwritten.
Instead, it is generated by a planner LLM based on task-specific
instructions provided as a prompt. The goal is to synthesize a program
$`f`$ that, given a training dataset of input and optional ground-truth
output pairs $`\mathrm{D}\subseteq T_{i}\times T_{o}`$ and a loss
function $`\mathsf{L}:T_{i}\times T_{o}\times T_{o}\to\mathbb{R}^{+}`$,
minimizes the aggregated loss
$`\tfrac{1}{|\mathrm{D}|}\sum_{(x_{i},y_{i})\in\mathrm{D}}\mathsf{L}(x_{i},y_{i},f(x_{i}))`$.
For certain tasks, the ground truth $`y_{i}`$ may not be available; in
such cases, the loss is denoted as $`\mathsf{L}(x_{i},\_,f(x_{i}))`$.
Assume that a context-free grammar (CFG) $`G`$ defines the set of
syntactically valid programs $`f`$ as $`L(G)\subseteq\Sigma^{*}`$. Given
the library functions $`\mathcal{F}`$, let $`\mathsf{S}(G,\mathcal{F})`$
denote the search space for $`f:T_{i}\to T_{o}`$ with type signature
$`(T_{i}\to T_{o})`$, including all parametric values of the models in
$`\mathcal{F}_{p}`$. Self-evolving agentic frameworks aim to find the
optimal solution $`{f}^{*}`$ to the following optimization problem.

|     |     |     |     |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| (1) |     |

````math
{f}^{*}=\argmin_{f\in\mathsf{S}(G,\mathcal{F})}\tfrac{1}{|\mathrm{D}|}\times{\textstyle\sum_{(x_{i},\_)\in\mathrm{D}}\mathsf{L}(x_{i},\_,f(x_{i}))}
``` |  |

## 3. Problem Formulation

High-level formulation of agent synthesis with formal constraints:
Eq. [1](#S2.E1 "In 2. Background ‣ SEVerA: Verified Self-Evolving Agents")
searches only for the optimal program $`{f}^{*}`$ that minimizes the
loss on the training set $`\mathrm{D}`$. However, it provides no
guarantee about how $`{f}^{*}`$ performs on unseen user inputs outside
$`\mathrm{D}`$. In contrast, deductive program synthesis ([Alur et al.,
2013](#bib.bib14); [Solar-Lezama, 2013](#bib.bib20)) allows program
generation to be controlled by formal behavioral input
$`\Phi:T_{i}\to\{T,F\}`$ and output specifications
$`\Psi:T_{i}\times T_{o}\to\{T,F\}`$. The use of formal behavioral
specifications
![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)
enables proving the correctness of the synthesized program for all
inputs that satisfy the input specification, and
![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)
can guide the search for $`{f}^{*}`$ by eliminating unverified program
candidates. With $`(\Phi,\Psi)`$, the unconstrained learning problem in
Eq. [1](#S2.E1 "In 2. Background ‣ SEVerA: Verified Self-Evolving Agents")
can be reformulated as the constrained learning problem shown below.

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
| (2) |  |
``` math
{f}^{*}=\argmin_{f\in\mathsf{S}(G,\mathcal{F})}\overbrace{\tfrac{1}{|\mathrm{D}|}\times{\textstyle\sum_{(x_{i},\_)\in\mathrm{D}}}\;\;\mathsf{L}(x_{i},\_,f(x_{i}))}^{\text{soft learning objective}}\;\;\text{s.t.}\;\;\overbrace{\forall x\in T_{i}.\;\Phi(x)\implies\Psi(x,f(x))}^{\text{hard formal constraints}}
``` |  |

The central question is whether
Eq. [2](#S3.E2 "In 3. Problem Formulation ‣ SEVerA: Verified Self-Evolving Agents")
can be solved while retaining the performance benefits and scalability
of gradient-based methods designed for
Eq. [1](#S2.E1 "In 2. Background ‣ SEVerA: Verified Self-Evolving Agents").
Next, we illustrate how practical constraints from several application
domains can be encoded as behavioral specifications $`(\Phi,\Psi)`$.

Examples of formal constraints $`(\Phi,\Psi)`$: The output specification
$`\Psi`$ characterizes the agent’s expected behavior on any valid input,
not just on examples in $`\mathrm{D}`$. Hard constraints therefore
detect and mitigate errors during synthesis that would not be revealed
by performance evaluation on a fixed dataset $`\mathrm{D}`$. We show
encodings of $`(\Phi,\Psi)`$ for four different tasks from distinct
domains.
![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)
Scientific Discovery: We consider constrained symbolic regression, where
the task is to recover an unknown mathematical formula from observed
data. The formal constraints $`(\Phi,\Psi)`$ encode prior knowledge
about the target formula, such as known symbolic bounds ([Błądek and
Krawiec, 2019](#bib.bib34); [Haider and Kronberger, 2022](#bib.bib41);
[Li et al., 2023](#bib.bib31)) or asymptotic behavior ([Li et al.,
2019](#bib.bib35)). Any generated formula that violates these hard
constraints is invalid, regardless of its empirical fit to the data.
Moreover, in the presence of noise, the constraints $`(\Phi,\Psi)`$ help
prevent overfitting, which cannot be addressed solely by optimizing a
soft objective ([Kronberger et al., 2022](#bib.bib28)).
![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)
Program Verification: Given a program in a verification-aware language
such as Dafny with a predefined specification, the agent is expected to
synthesize annotations (e.g., loop invariants, assertions, ranking
functions) ([Loughridge et al., 2025](#bib.bib36); [Sun et al.,
2024](#bib.bib38); [Mugnier et al., 2025](#bib.bib37)). Task success
depends on whether the annotated program verifies. Recent work
([Banerjee et al., 2026](#bib.bib44)) shows that agents using frontier
models (e.g., Claude) may cheat by subtly modifying the input program,
such as altering variable initializations, instead of producing correct
annotations. ([Banerjee et al., 2026](#bib.bib44)) reports that such
modifications were not detected by prior string-based checkers, leading
to inflated task accuracy. In contrast, formal AST-based diff checkers
that syntactically enforce equivalence between the input program and the
annotated output serve as hard constraints, ensuring the agent cannot
cheat even on unseen inputs.
![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)
Constrained LLM Generation: Constrained generation captures a class of
problems in which LLMs are required to generate strings that follow a
formal structure. Typically, these formal structures are defined using
formal grammars (regular ([Suresh et al., 2025](#bib.bib26)) or
context-free grammars ([Ugare et al., 2025b](#bib.bib24); [Park et al.,
2024](#bib.bib25))), or static analyzers such as type checkers ([Mündler
et al., 2025](#bib.bib42); [Nagy et al., 2026](#bib.bib43)). In our
setting, these formal structures define the output specification
$`\Psi`$. We consider the task of generating symbolic math expressions
from natural language questions, where hard constraints ensure that the
synthesized agent always produces at least a structurally valid
expression.
![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)
Agentic Tool Use: Conversational LLM agents deployed in customer-service
settings must select and invoke API tools to resolve user requests while
respecting domain-specific policies, such as refund eligibility,
booking-modification rules, and authentication-before-access
requirements ([Barres et al., 2025](#bib.bib49)). These temporal and
logical policy constraints can be expressed as formal specifications
that govern the ordering and content of agent actions. Agent-C ([Kamath
et al., 2025](#bib.bib29)) provides a domain-specific language for
specifying such temporal properties and translates them into linear
temporal logic (LTL), enabling SMT-based checking of the generated tool
calls. Crucially, the hard constraint is enforced at each individual
tool call: given the current tool-call trace, the Agent-C checker
verifies whether the next proposed tool call complies with the defined
formal policy before it is executed. Task performance (utility), in
contrast, is measured over the entire multi-turn interaction trace as
whether the agent successfully resolves the user request. In our
formulation, $`\Psi`$ uses the Agent-C checker to define a hard
constraint applied to each tool call, ensuring that synthesized agents
never violate domain policies at any step, regardless of user input.
Overall, hard behavioral constraints capture the minimal requirements
that synthesized agents must satisfy on all inputs, thereby enabling the
pruning of untrusted candidates during synthesis.

## 4. Overview

![Refer to caption](2603.25111v2/figs/agentassure_overview.png)

Figure 1. Overview of SEVerA, which operates in three key steps. (1)
Search: Given the task information, library functions
$`\mathcal{F}_{c}`$, a list of parametric generative models (GMs)
$`\mathcal{F}_{p}`$, and specifications $`(\Phi,\Psi)`$, the planner LLM
outputs a parametric agentic program in which all formal output
specifications of GM calls are defined using the FGGM setup. (2) Verify:
Given the parametric agentic code, this step first verifies all FGGM
definitions proposed by the planner. Once verified, it uses their local
contracts to check the program against $`(\Phi,\Psi)`$. If all checks
pass, the program is accepted and the unconstrained learning step is
invoked on the verified program; otherwise, an error message is returned
to the planner. (3) Learn: This step optimizes the parameters of the
underlying GMs within each FGGM to improve conformance with local
contracts defined in step (1), while also reducing the task-loss
$`\mathsf{L}{}`$ over the dataset $`\mathrm{D}`$. After tuning, SEVerA
maintains a pool of verified fine-tuned agents and uses their execution
traces on $`\mathrm{D}`$ to generate new candidates via step (1). All
agents in the pool are valid candidate solutions, and the one with the
lowest $`\mathsf{L}{}`$ on $`\mathrm{D}`$ is returned. Central to SEVerA
is the Formally Guarded Generative Model (FGGM), which binds each GM
call to local input–output contracts $`(\Phi_{l},\Psi_{l})`$ and a
verified non-parametric fallback, ensuring that the contracts hold
irrespective of the underlying GM parameters. This enables unconstrained
gradient-based parameter optimization without compromising formal
correctness.

Fig. [1](#S4.F1 "Figure 1 ‣ 4. Overview ‣ SEVerA: Verified Self-Evolving Agents")
gives a high-level overview of SEVerA for solving the constrained
learning problem in
Eq. [2](#S3.E2 "In 3. Problem Formulation ‣ SEVerA: Verified Self-Evolving Agents")
over the search space $`\mathsf{S}(G,\mathcal{F})`$. In this setting, we
need to simultaneously optimize task-specific performance while
guaranteeing that the resulting program provably satisfies the given
behavioral constraints. This is difficult because the search space
contains both discrete program structure and continuous model
parameters, and because although GMs such as LLMs are powerful, they are
inherently unreliable, which makes it hard to ensure conformance with
behavioral specifications.

To address these challenges, SEVerA retains the best of both worlds:
constraint-guided program search from deductive synthesis and
unconstrained gradient-based parameter optimization. Specifically,
SEVerA employs a CEGIS-style loop in which a planner LLM proposes
candidate parametric programs and a verifier checks their correctness
with respect to the behavioral specification. Once a parametric program
is verified, SEVerA applies unconstrained gradient-based optimization to
tune the underlying GM parameters and reduce the task-specific loss
$`\mathsf{L}{}`$. The proposed Formally Guarded Generative Model (FGGM)
serves as the critical link between these two strategies. The FGGM setup
allows one to bind each GM call to explicit local input–output contracts
and a verified non-parametric fallback program, ensuring that these
contracts hold regardless of the underlying GM parameters. The verifier
then leverages these local contracts to prove the correctness of the
parametric program with respect to the behavioral specification. Beyond
providing correctness guarantees, these contracts also extract local
learning objectives by characterizing the expected outputs of each GM
call. This enables gradient-based optimization to improve the GM’s
conformance to its local contracts, thereby connecting constrained
program search with unconstrained learning.

Next, we discuss the components of SEVerA through two representative and
easy-to-understand problem instances from different domains: scientific
discovery and program verification.

### 4.1. Example Instantiation of SEVerA

#### 4.1.1. Constrained Symbolic Regression:

In symbolic regression, each problem instance consists of possibly noisy
observations of input–output pairs generated by an unknown ground-truth
function $`f_{gt}`$. The goal is to recover this ground-truth function
from the training data $`\mathrm{D}`$, a popular task in scientific
discovery and neuro-symbolic program synthesis ([Shojaee et al.,
2025](#bib.bib16); [Ellis et al., 2021](#bib.bib39)). In constrained
symbolic regression ([Błądek and Krawiec, 2019](#bib.bib34); [Haider and
Kronberger, 2022](#bib.bib41)), users encode known properties of
$`f_{gt}`$ beyond what is captured in $`\mathrm{D}`$ as formal
constraints, ensuring that the recovered function $`f`$ satisfies these
constraints. This setup directly follows the constrained learning
formulation in
Eq. [2](#S3.E2 "In 3. Problem Formulation ‣ SEVerA: Verified Self-Evolving Agents"),
where the synthesized agent $`{f}^{*}`$ corresponds to the recovered
function. For illustration, we consider the problem instance with
ground-truth function $`f_{gt}(x)=\sqrt{1.23\times\max(x,0.0)}`$, taken
from ([Li et al., 2023](#bib.bib31)). The dataset $`\mathrm{D}`$
contains input–output pairs $`(x,y)\in\mathbb{R}^{2}`$, where
$`y=f_{gt}(x)+\epsilon`$ is a noisy observation of $`f_{gt}(x)`$ and
$`\epsilon\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\sigma)`$ denotes additive Gaussian noise.
The pointwise loss function $`\mathsf{L}{}`$ is the commonly used
Normalized Mean Squared Error (NMSE) (see
Eq. [3](#S4.E3 "In 4.1.1. Constrained Symbolic Regression: ‣ 4.1. Example Instantiation of SEVerA ‣ 4. Overview ‣ SEVerA: Verified Self-Evolving Agents")).
For this instance, the agent’s type signature $`\tau`$ is
$`(\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R})`$, and the behavioral specifications
$`(\Phi,\Psi)`$ define known symbolic bounds on $`f_{gt}`$ (see
Eq. [4](#S4.E4 "In 4.1.1. Constrained Symbolic Regression: ‣ 4.1. Example Instantiation of SEVerA ‣ 4. Overview ‣ SEVerA: Verified Self-Evolving Agents"))
where $`{\color[rgb]{0.293,0,0.5117}sqrt}:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}`$ is a
provided library function.

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
| (3) |  |
``` math
\mathsf{L}{}(x_{i},y_{i},f(x_{i}))=\tfrac{(f(x_{i})-y_{i})^{2}}{C}\;\;\text{where ${\textstyle C=\sum_{(x_{i},y_{i})\in\mathrm{D}}y_{i}^{2}}$}
``` |  |

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
| (4) |  |
``` math
\Phi(x):\;(x\geq 0),\;\Psi(x,f(x)):\;\left((x\leq 1)\implies(f(x)\geq{\color[rgb]{0.293,0,0.5117}pow}(x,0.8)\right)\wedge\left((x\geq 1)\implies(f(x)\geq{\color[rgb]{0.293,0,0.5117}sqrt}((x))\right)
``` |  |

Search Space: SEVerA defines the search space using a restricted subset
of Dafny supporting four basic types
$`\{{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}int},{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}bool},{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}real},{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}str}\}`$,
conditional blocks, while loops, and function calls. We formalize the
search space in
§ [5.1](#S5.SS1 "5.1. Search Space ‣ 5. Technical Details ‣ SEVerA: Verified Self-Evolving Agents").

Library Functions: For this task, the library function set
$`\mathcal{F}`$ includes common transcendental functions (e.g.,
$`{\color[rgb]{0.293,0,0.5117}sin}`$,
$`{\color[rgb]{0.293,0,0.5117}cos}`$,
$`{\color[rgb]{0.293,0,0.5117}pow}`$,
$`{\color[rgb]{0.293,0,0.5117}sqrt}`$) as well as small parametric
neural networks (NNs), enabling the search space to capture a wide range
of neuro-symbolic programs. Users provide type signatures and formal
contracts for all non-parametric library functions; the planner LLM
defines formal contracts for each parametric model call through the FGGM
setup
(§ [4.2](#S4.SS2 "4.2. Formally Guarded Generative Model ‣ 4. Overview ‣ SEVerA: Verified Self-Evolving Agents")).
We present representative type signatures and specifications in
Eq. [5](#S4.E5 "In 4.1.1. Constrained Symbolic Regression: ‣ 4.1. Example Instantiation of SEVerA ‣ 4. Overview ‣ SEVerA: Verified Self-Evolving Agents"),
with the complete set in
Appendix [C](#A3 "Appendix C Library Functions for Symbolic Regression ‣ SEVerA: Verified Self-Evolving Agents").

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
| (5) |  |
``` math
{\color[rgb]{0.293,0,0.5117}sqrt}(x:{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}real})\to{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}real},\;\Phi_{sqrt}(x):(x\geq 0),\;\Psi_{sqrt}(x,{\color[rgb]{0.293,0,0.5117}sqrt}(x)):({\color[rgb]{0.293,0,0.5117}sqrt}(x)\geq 0);\;\;{\textstyle{\color[rgb]{0.293,0,0.5117}NN^{(1)}_{\theta}}(x_{1}:{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}real})}\to{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}real}
``` |  |

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
| (6) |  |
``` math
\forall x,d_{1},d_{2}\in\mathbb{R}.(x\geq 1)\wedge(d_{1}\geq d_{2})\implies{\color[rgb]{0.293,0,0.5117}pow}(x,d_{1})\geq{\color[rgb]{0.293,0,0.5117}pow}(x,d_{2})
``` |  |

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
| (7) |  |
``` math
\forall x,d_{1},d_{2}\in\mathbb{R}.(x\leq 1)\wedge(d_{1}\geq d_{2})\implies{\color[rgb]{0.293,0,0.5117}pow}(x,d_{1})\leq{\color[rgb]{0.293,0,0.5117}pow}(x,d_{2})
``` |  |

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
| (8) |  |
``` math
\;\varphi_{\mathcal{A}}\implies\forall x\in T_{i}.\big(\Phi(x)\implies\Psi(x,f(x))\big)\;\;\text{where $\varphi_{\mathcal{A}{}}=({\textstyle\bigwedge_{\varphi\in\mathcal{A}}\;}\varphi)$}
``` |  |

Axioms: The axioms $`\mathcal{A}`$ encode known properties of library
functions in $`\mathcal{F}`$, including their formal contracts as
universally quantified first-order sentences, where library functions
are treated as uninterpreted. For example,
Eq. [7](#S4.E7 "In 4.1.1. Constrained Symbolic Regression: ‣ 4.1. Example Instantiation of SEVerA ‣ 4. Overview ‣ SEVerA: Verified Self-Evolving Agents")
captures a property of $`{\color[rgb]{0.293,0,0.5117}pow}`$. These
axioms assist automated verification as shown in
Eq. [8](#S4.E8 "In 4.1.1. Constrained Symbolic Regression: ‣ 4.1. Example Instantiation of SEVerA ‣ 4. Overview ‣ SEVerA: Verified Self-Evolving Agents").
We provide the formal syntax for defining $`\mathcal{A}`$ in
§ [5.1](#S5.SS1 "5.1. Search Space ‣ 5. Technical Details ‣ SEVerA: Verified Self-Evolving Agents")
and the complete axiom set for this task in
Appendix [D](#A4 "Appendix D Additional Axioms for Symbolic Regression ‣ SEVerA: Verified Self-Evolving Agents").

Like other synthesis frameworks with library functions ([Feng et al.,
2017](#bib.bib21)), SEVerA assumes that all library functions have
correct input–output specifications, and that they are pure and
terminating. Verifying the correctness of the library functions and
axioms is outside the scope of SEVerA.

#### 4.1.2. LLM-Assisted Automated Verification

This task aims to synthesize annotations, such as inductive loop
invariants, ranking functions, and assertions, that enable automatic
verification and termination checking of input Dafny programs with
pre-encoded input–output specifications ([Sun et al., 2024](#bib.bib38);
[Loughridge et al., 2025](#bib.bib36)). The agent has type signature
$`(p:{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}str})\to{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}str}`$, mapping an
input Dafny program with pre-encoded specifications, represented as a
string, to an annotated Dafny program. The point-wise loss function
$`\mathsf{L}{}`$ evaluates whether the annotated program verifies within
a pre-fixed time budget, assigning $`1`$ to unverified programs and
$`0`$ to verified ones
(Eq. [10](#S4.E10 "In 4.1.2. LLM-Assisted Automated Verification ‣ 4.1. Example Instantiation of SEVerA ‣ 4. Overview ‣ SEVerA: Verified Self-Evolving Agents")).
Hard constraints $`(\Phi,\Psi)`$ ensure that, for any parsable input
program, the output remains parsable and does not change the input
program beyond adding annotations
(Eq. [11](#S4.E11 "In 4.1.2. LLM-Assisted Automated Verification ‣ 4.1. Example Instantiation of SEVerA ‣ 4. Overview ‣ SEVerA: Verified Self-Evolving Agents")).
We use the Dafny built-in verifier to define $`\mathsf{L}{}`$, and the
Dafny parser together with the AST-based formal diff checker from
([Banerjee et al., 2026](#bib.bib44)) to define $`(\Phi,\Psi)`$.
$`{\color[rgb]{0.293,0,0.5117}noDiff}`$ returns True if the second input
program is syntactically equivalent to the first (ignoring annotations),
and False otherwise. The library function set $`\mathcal{F}`$ includes
all these components. Although parsing and diff checks could be
incorporated into $`\mathsf{L}{}`$ by penalizing invalid outputs on
$`\mathrm{D}`$, these constraints must hold for all possible inputs, not
only those in $`\mathrm{D}`$. Therefore, any candidate agent that fails
to satisfy them must be filtered out.

Library Functions: We use the same search space as constrained symbolic
regression. $`\mathcal{F}`$ includes the verifier with a pre-fixed time
budget $`{\color[rgb]{0.293,0,0.5117}verify}`$, the Dafny parser
$`{\color[rgb]{0.293,0,0.5117}parse}`$, the diff-checker
$`{\color[rgb]{0.293,0,0.5117}noDiff}`$. We show the type signature and
formal contract of representative functions in
Eq. [9](#S4.E9 "In 4.1.2. LLM-Assisted Automated Verification ‣ 4.1. Example Instantiation of SEVerA ‣ 4. Overview ‣ SEVerA: Verified Self-Evolving Agents")
while providing the rest in
Appendix [E](#A5 "Appendix E Library Functions for Dafny Program Verification ‣ SEVerA: Verified Self-Evolving Agents").

|  |  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|----|
| (9) |  |  | $`\displaystyle{\color[rgb]{0.293,0,0.5117}noDiff}(\boldsymbol{x}:{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}str},\boldsymbol{y}:{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}str})\to{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}bool},\;\Phi(\boldsymbol{x},\boldsymbol{y}):{\color[rgb]{0.293,0,0.5117}parse}(\boldsymbol{x}),\;\Psi(\boldsymbol{x},\boldsymbol{y},{\color[rgb]{0.293,0,0.5117}noDiff}(\boldsymbol{x},\boldsymbol{y})):T`$ |  |
| (10) |  |  | $`\displaystyle\mathsf{L}{}(\boldsymbol{x},\_,\boldsymbol{y})=1-\mathbb{I}({\color[rgb]{0.293,0,0.5117}parse}(\boldsymbol{y})\wedge{\color[rgb]{0.293,0,0.5117}noDiff}(\boldsymbol{x},\boldsymbol{y})\wedge{\color[rgb]{0.293,0,0.5117}verify}(\boldsymbol{y}))`$ |  |
| (11) |  |  | $`\displaystyle\Phi(\boldsymbol{x}):{\color[rgb]{0.293,0,0.5117}parse}(\boldsymbol{x});\;\Psi(\boldsymbol{x},f(\boldsymbol{x})):{\color[rgb]{0.293,0,0.5117}parse}(f(\boldsymbol{x}))\wedge{\color[rgb]{0.293,0,0.5117}noDiff}(\boldsymbol{x},f(\boldsymbol{x}))`$ |  |

Axioms: Example of a first-order sentence encoding known properties of
$`{\color[rgb]{0.293,0,0.5117}noDiff}`$ in
Eq. [12](#S4.E12 "In 4.1.2. LLM-Assisted Automated Verification ‣ 4.1. Example Instantiation of SEVerA ‣ 4. Overview ‣ SEVerA: Verified Self-Evolving Agents").
$`{\color[rgb]{0.293,0,0.5117}noDiff}`$ is both reflexive and transitive
w.r.t all parsable Dafny programs. It is easy to see that same program
will always have no difference with itself. We list all the axioms in
Appendix [F](#A6 "Appendix F Additional Axioms for Dafny Program Verification ‣ SEVerA: Verified Self-Evolving Agents").

|  |  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|----|
| (12) |  |  | $`\displaystyle\textbf{Reflexivity:}\;\;\forall\boldsymbol{x}\in\Sigma^{*}.\;{\color[rgb]{0.293,0,0.5117}parse}(\boldsymbol{x})\implies{\color[rgb]{0.293,0,0.5117}noDiff}(\boldsymbol{x},\boldsymbol{x})`$ |  |

### 4.2. Formally Guarded Generative Model

Formally Guarded Generative Model (FGGM) setup allows the planner LLM to
bind each generative model (GM) call to local input–output contracts
$`(\Phi_{l},\Psi_{l})`$ that formally characterize the output. Once the
FGGM is verified to be well-formed, the defined contracts can be used to
prove the correctness of the agentic program against the behavioral
specifications $`(\Phi,\Psi)`$. Our FGGM design ensures the following
essential properties.
![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)
*Flexibility:* Unlike functions in $`\mathcal{F}_{c}`$, output contracts
cannot be predefined by users because the expected output of a GM varies
across calls depending on the prompt. In our design, the planner LLM
synthesizes custom first-order formulas over terms involving
non-parametric functions (e.g., sqrt) and predicates (e.g.,
$`{\color[rgb]{0.293,0,0.5117}noDiff}`$) from $`\mathcal{F}_{c}`$ to
specify local contracts.
![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)
*Parameter-Independent Correctness:* Provided the defined FGGM is
well-formed, the specified contracts hold irrespective of the parameters
of the underlying GM. This property is crucial to ensure that
gradient-based parameter optimization never breaks the correctness
guarantees.
![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)
*Local Learning Objective:* Although correctness holds irrespective of
parameter values, the local contracts $`(\Phi_{l},\Psi_{l})`$ extract
the local learning objective for a particular GM call by characterizing
its expected output. This objective can guide gradient-based
optimization so that, after tuning, the GM’s conformance with
$`(\Phi_{l},\Psi_{l})`$ improves
(§ [4.2.3](#S4.SS2.SSS3 "4.2.3. Conformance Tuning ‣ 4.2. Formally Guarded Generative Model ‣ 4. Overview ‣ SEVerA: Verified Self-Evolving Agents")).

#### 4.2.1. Intuition

For each FGGM with local contracts $`(\Phi_{l},\Psi_{l})`$ and
underlying parametric GM $`\mathcal{L}_{\Theta}`$, the planner LLM
synthesizes two non-parametric programs using only functions from
$`\mathcal{F}_{c}`$. The first is a fallback program $`f_{d}`$ that
satisfies $`(\Phi_{l},\Psi_{l})`$ and guards against edge cases in which
the GM hallucinates or produces outputs that violate the specification.
Without a verified fallback, the rejection sampler could exhaust all
samples; the fallback is what makes the contract hold unconditionally
for all parameter values. Intuitively, although $`f_{d}`$ may lack the
GM’s task-solving capability (low task performance), it prevents the
candidate agent from entering unsafe program states during execution
(high constraint satisfaction). The second is a prompting program
$`f_{p}`$, which constructs the input to the GM (which may be just a
neural network). For LLMs, $`f_{p}`$ encodes task-specific
natural-language instructions, analogous to prompt-tuning techniques
([Khattab et al., 2024](#bib.bib33); [Beurer-Kellner et al.,
2023](#bib.bib32)) known to improve GM performance and instruction
adherence. Once the planner LLM proposes $`\Phi_{l},\Psi_{l},f_{p},`$
and $`f_{d}`$, SEVerA automatically constructs a rejection sampler that
treats outputs of underlying GM as samples from a proposal distribution
$`\pi_{p}`$ for an input $`\boldsymbol{p}`$. The local specifications
$`(\Phi_{l},\Psi_{l})`$ define the support set
(Definition [2.2](#S2.Thmtheorem2 "Definition 2.2. ‣ 2. Background ‣ SEVerA: Verified Self-Evolving Agents"))
of the target distribution $`\pi_{t}`$ on $`\boldsymbol{p}`$, assigning
zero probability to outputs that violate $`(\Phi_{l},\Psi_{l})`$. The
rejection sampler draws a fixed number $`K\geq 1`$ of samples from
$`\mathcal{L}_{\Theta}`$, as specified by the user, and falls back to
$`f_{d}`$ if all samples are rejected
(Fig [2](#S4.F2 "Figure 2 ‣ 4.2.1. Intuition ‣ 4.2. Formally Guarded Generative Model ‣ 4. Overview ‣ SEVerA: Verified Self-Evolving Agents")).
The purpose of $`f_{p}`$ and optional conformance tuning is to improve
the acceptance rate of the rejection sampler for any input, thereby
reducing reliance on the fallback $`f_{d}`$. We formally define the FGGM
syntax, well-formedness conditions, and the computability of the output
checker in
§ [5.2.1](#S5.SS2.SSS1 "5.2.1. FGGM Formal Definition ‣ 5.2. Key Steps ‣ 5. Technical Details ‣ SEVerA: Verified Self-Evolving Agents").

#### 4.2.2. Examples

We show a couple of example FGGM definitions that the planner LLM
suggests: one from symbolic regression and one from Dafny program
verification. The first example from symbolic regression
(Eq. [13](#S4.E13 "In 4.2.2. Examples ‣ 4.2. Formally Guarded Generative Model ‣ 4. Overview ‣ SEVerA: Verified Self-Evolving Agents"))
with id $`{\color[rgb]{0.293,0,0.5117}boundedParam}`$, type signature
$`(l:{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}real},u:{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}real})\to{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}real}`$,
underlying parametric GM which is a neural network
$`NN^{(2)}_{\Theta}:\mathbb{R}^{2}\to\mathbb{R}`$ for this case,
$`\Phi_{l}:(l\leq u)`$ $`\Psi_{l}`$
(Eq. [13](#S4.E13 "In 4.2.2. Examples ‣ 4.2. Formally Guarded Generative Model ‣ 4. Overview ‣ SEVerA: Verified Self-Evolving Agents"))
restricts $`{\color[rgb]{0.293,0,0.5117}boundedParam}(l,u)`$ to lie
within $`[l,u]`$. The fallback clamps any violating sample $`y`$ using
library functions $`{\color[rgb]{0.293,0,0.5117}min}`$ and
$`{\color[rgb]{0.293,0,0.5117}max}`$, ensuring contract preservation.

The second example from Dafny program verification
(Eq. [14](#S4.E14 "In 4.2.2. Examples ‣ 4.2. Formally Guarded Generative Model ‣ 4. Overview ‣ SEVerA: Verified Self-Evolving Agents"))
with id $`{\color[rgb]{0.293,0,0.5117}dafnyAnnotate}`$, type signature
$`(p:{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}str})\to{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}str}`$, underlying
parametric GM which is a LLM
$`\mathcal{L}_{\Theta}:\Sigma^{*}\to\Sigma^{*}`$,
$`\Phi_{l}:{\color[rgb]{0.293,0,0.5117}parse}(p)`$, $`\Psi_{l}`$
(Eq. [14](#S4.E14 "In 4.2.2. Examples ‣ 4.2. Formally Guarded Generative Model ‣ 4. Overview ‣ SEVerA: Verified Self-Evolving Agents"))
ensures $`{\color[rgb]{0.293,0,0.5117}dafnyAnnotate}(p)`$ always outputs
a syntactically valid program and only adds annotations to the input
program $`p`$. If all samples are rejected, the fallback safely returns
the original program $`p`$, guaranteeing $`\Psi_{l}`$ under $`\Phi_{l}`$
utilizing the reflexivity axiom
(Eq [12](#S4.E12 "In 4.1.2. LLM-Assisted Automated Verification ‣ 4.1. Example Instantiation of SEVerA ‣ 4. Overview ‣ SEVerA: Verified Self-Evolving Agents")).
These examples show how a planner LLM can define FGGMs with fallbacks to
avoid incorrect program states for diverse tasks.
````
