\lx@text@lbrace{\color[rgb]{0,0.3594,0.668}{return}}\ ${\color[rgb]{0.293,0,0.5117}min}({\color[rgb]{0.293,0,0.5117}max}(l,y),u)$;\lx@text@rbrace}`$ |  |
| (14) |  | $`\displaystyle\Psi_{l}`$ | $`\displaystyle:\ {\color[rgb]{0.293,0,0.5117}parse}(p)\wedge{\color[rgb]{0.293,0,0.5117}noDiff}(p,f(p)),`$ | $`\displaystyle f_{d}`$ | $`\displaystyle:\ \text{
{\color[rgb]{0,0.3594,0.668}{function}}\ {\color[rgb]{0.293,0,0.5117}$f_{d}$}(p:{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}str}, y:{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}str}) $:({\color[rgb]{0,0,1}str})$
\lx@text@lbrace{\color[rgb]{0,0.3594,0.668}{return}}\ $p$;\lx@text@rbrace}`$ |  |

Design Considerations. Alternative approaches for enforcing formal
constraints on generative model calls exist, but they fall short of
FGGM. Constrained decoding ([Ugare et al., 2025b](#bib.bib24); [Park et
al., 2024](#bib.bib25); [Nagy et al., 2026](#bib.bib43); [Banerjee et
al., 2025](#bib.bib45)) modifies the model’s internal decoding
procedure, which limits its applicability to open-source models and
restricts constraints to syntactic forms such as context-free grammars.
Post-hoc output filtering without a fallback provides no guarantees: if
all sampled outputs are rejected, the program produces no valid output.
Fully verifying an agentic program is computationally intractable, as it
depends on large parametric components such as LLMs. FGGM addresses all
three limitations: it operates solely on model outputs, making it
compatible with closed-source models; it incorporates a verified
fallback that guarantees a valid output on every execution; and it
decomposes verification into parameter-independent local contracts.
Moreover, these local contracts can be utilized during learning to guide
parameter tuning, improving conformance, and reducing reliance on the
fallback.

#### 4.2.3. Conformance Tuning

A FGGM that always uses the fallback is formally correct but practically
no better than a non-parametric program $`f_{d}`$, conformance tuning
helps avoid this by teaching the GM to satisfy the defined contract
directly. The local contracts $`(\Phi_{l},\Psi_{l})`$ define the local
learning objective to avoid the fallback and assign higher probability
to outputs that pass the check
$`{\color[rgb]{0.293,0,0.5117}check_{\mathcal{A},\Phi_{l},\Psi_{l}}}`$.
The objective in
Eq. [20](#S5.E20 "In 5.2.5. Learn ‣ 5.2. Key Steps ‣ 5. Technical Details ‣ SEVerA: Verified Self-Evolving Agents")
minimizes the expected contract violation of GM samples over an input
set $`\mathbb{P}`$. For any $`\theta\in\Theta`$, the inner term
$`\mathsf{L}_{\Phi_{l},\Psi_{l}}^{\theta}(p)`$ measures the probability
that a sampled output from $`\mathcal{L}_{\theta}(p)`$ violates
$`{\color[rgb]{0.293,0,0.5117}check_{\mathcal{A},\Phi_{l},\Psi_{l}}}(\Phi_{l},\Psi_{l},x_{1},\dots,x_{n},y)`$,
while $`\mathsf{L}_{\Phi_{l},\Psi_{l}}(\theta)`$ aggregates this
violation across inputs in $`\mathbb{P}`$. By optimizing
$`\theta\in\Theta`$ to reduce this loss, the GM post-tuning is
encouraged to concentrate the probability mass on the support defined by
$`(\Phi_{l},\Psi_{l})`$ (details in
§ [5.2.5](#S5.SS2.SSS5 "5.2.5. Learn ‣ 5.2. Key Steps ‣ 5. Technical Details ‣ SEVerA: Verified Self-Evolving Agents")).
Overall conformance tuning improves the acceptance rate of the rejection
sampler, reducing reliance on $`f_{d}`$. We formalize the conformance
loss in
§ [5.2.5](#S5.SS2.SSS5 "5.2.5. Learn ‣ 5.2. Key Steps ‣ 5. Technical Details ‣ SEVerA: Verified Self-Evolving Agents")
(Eq. [20](#S5.E20 "In 5.2.5. Learn ‣ 5.2. Key Steps ‣ 5. Technical Details ‣ SEVerA: Verified Self-Evolving Agents")).

### 4.3. SEVerA

SEVerA employs a three-step strategy to solve the constrained learning
problem in
Eq. [2](#S3.E2 "In 3. Problem Formulation ‣ SEVerA: Verified Self-Evolving Agents"):

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

(a) Unverified parametric program pruned out.

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

(b) Verified parametric program.

Figure 3. Two example candidate parametric programs generated for
symbolic regression.

(1) Search: The planner LLM defines FGGMs with their prompting programs
$`f_{p}`$, then samples candidate parametric programs that invoke these
FGGMs. Direct calls to parametric GMs are disallowed; each must be
wrapped within a verified FGGM.

(2) Verify: SEVerA checks all FGGM definitions for well-formedness and
then verifies the candidate program against $`(\Phi,\Psi)`$ using the
Dafny built-in verifier. If verification fails, error feedback is
returned to the planner LLM to refine the candidate (CEGIS-style loop).
Due to the FGGM setup, any verified program satisfies the behavioral
specifications for all parameter values. (3) Learn: The learning step
applies unconstrained gradient-based optimization to tune GM parameters,
guided by the global task loss $`\mathsf{L}{}`$ and local conformance
losses from each FGGM. For closed-source LLMs without accessible
parameters, the learning step is skipped and improvements rely on prompt
tuning through $`f_{p}`$. We formalize the search-verify-learn loop in
§ [5.2](#S5.SS2 "5.2. Key Steps ‣ 5. Technical Details ‣ SEVerA: Verified Self-Evolving Agents")
(Algorithms [1](#alg1 "Algorithm 1 ‣ 5.2.3. Computability of 𝑐⁢ℎ⁢𝑒⁢𝑐⁢𝑘_{𝒜,Φ_𝑙,Ψ_𝑙} (Fig. ) on concrete values ‣ 5.2. Key Steps ‣ 5. Technical Details ‣ SEVerA: Verified Self-Evolving Agents")
and [2](#alg2 "Algorithm 2 ‣ 5.2.6. SEVerA ‣ 5.2. Key Steps ‣ 5. Technical Details ‣ SEVerA: Verified Self-Evolving Agents")).

#### 4.3.1. Candidate Pool and Execution Feedback

SEVerA maintains a pool of verified candidate agentic programs with
fine-tuned parameters
(Fig. [1](#S4.F1 "Figure 1 ‣ 4. Overview ‣ SEVerA: Verified Self-Evolving Agents")).
SEVerA selects the best-performing candidate agent from the pool, i.e.,
the one with the minimal task loss $`\mathsf{L}{}`$, and uses its
execution traces on data $`\mathrm{D}`$ to iteratively search for new
candidates via the planner LLM. The number of parametric candidate
sampling steps is capped by the user. Once this limit is reached, SEVerA
returns the agent in the pool with the lowest task loss
$`\mathsf{L}{}`$.
Fig. [3](#S4.F3 "Figure 3 ‣ 4.3. SEVerA ‣ 4. Overview ‣ SEVerA: Verified Self-Evolving Agents")
shows two candidate parametric programs sampled by the planner LLM. Each
program invokes the FGGM defined in
Eq. [13](#S4.E13 "In 4.2.2. Examples ‣ 4.2. Formally Guarded Generative Model ‣ 4. Overview ‣ SEVerA: Verified Self-Evolving Agents")
with id $`{\color[rgb]{0.293,0,0.5117}boundedParam}`$ from two different
locations.
Fig. [3(a)](#S4.F3.sf1 "In Figure 3 ‣ 4.3. SEVerA ‣ 4. Overview ‣ SEVerA: Verified Self-Evolving Agents")
shows the first parametric program, which fails to verify against the
behavioral specification and is therefore pruned by the verifier. This
candidate represents the output as a parametric affine function of the
input $`x`$, which does not match the ground truth, illustrating how
strict behavioral constraints eliminate poor candidates. The second
candidate verifies for all parameters of the neural networks
$`{\color[rgb]{0.293,0,0.5117}NN^{(2)}_{\Theta}}`$ wrapped inside the
$`{\color[rgb]{0.293,0,0.5117}boundedParam}`$ calls. After parameter
tuning, it recovers the ground truth with negligible error, as discussed
below. Currently, SEVerA does not share parameters across FGGM calls at
different locations and instead assigns separate parameter sets to each
$`{\color[rgb]{0.293,0,0.5117}boundedParam}`$ call. This design allows
the system to potentially learn different parameters at different call
sites to improve task-specific performance. Since both
$`{\color[rgb]{0.293,0,0.5117}boundedParam}`$ calls receive constant
inputs, after fine-tuning they return constant values, i.e., $`a=1.11`$
and $`d=0.503`$. This recovers the ground-truth function
$`\sqrt{1.23\times\max(x,0)}`$ with negligible error. Note that SEVerA
currently neither shares parameters nor caps the number of FGGM calls.
However, SEVerA can be extended to support both these checks to reduce
the computational budget required for parameter learning, as discussed
in
§ [6.5](#S6.SS5 "6.5. Discussion ‣ 6. Evaluation ‣ SEVerA: Verified Self-Evolving Agents").
The parametric candidate programs and all FGGM definitions with
synthesized prompting programs $`f_{p}{}`$ for the program verification
task are included in
Appendix [K](#A11 "Appendix K Example Agents for LLM Assisted Program Verification ‣ SEVerA: Verified Self-Evolving Agents").

In the next section, we formalize the search space, provide complete
algorithmic details for each step, and establish theoretical guarantees
for the framework.

## 5. Technical Details

We formalize the search space in
§ [5.1](#S5.SS1 "5.1. Search Space ‣ 5. Technical Details ‣ SEVerA: Verified Self-Evolving Agents"),
provide the details of the steps search, verify, and learn along with
FGGM in
§ [5.2](#S5.SS2 "5.2. Key Steps ‣ 5. Technical Details ‣ SEVerA: Verified Self-Evolving Agents").
We provide formal proof of soundness and a sufficient condition for
agent synthesis success with non-trivial utility in
§ [5.3](#S5.SS3 "5.3. Theoretical Results ‣ 5. Technical Details ‣ SEVerA: Verified Self-Evolving Agents").

### 5.1. Search Space

Program Search Space: We use a restricted subset of the popular
verification-aware language Dafny ([Leino, 2010](#bib.bib30)) to define
the search space of candidate programs. In this restricted subset, we
allow conditional blocks, while loops, assignment statements, assertion
statements, function calls, and annotations including invariant clauses
and ranking functions (decreases clauses), along with first-order
input–output specifications. We present the BNF grammar $`G_{D}`$
capturing this subset in
Appendix [A](#A1 "Appendix A Restricted Dafny Grammar ‣ SEVerA: Verified Self-Evolving Agents").
We allow four basic types
$`\mathsf{T}=\{{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}bool},{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}int},{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}real},{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}string}\}`$,
basic built-in arithmetic functions
$`\mathcal{B}_{a}=\{{\color[rgb]{0.293,0,0.5117}+},{\color[rgb]{0.293,0,0.5117}-},{\color[rgb]{0.293,0,0.5117}\times},{\color[rgb]{0.293,0,0.5117}/}\}`$,
boolean functions
$`\mathcal{B}_{b}=\{{\color[rgb]{0.293,0,0.5117}\&\&},{\color[rgb]{0.293,0,0.5117}||},{\color[rgb]{0.293,0,0.5117}!},{\color[rgb]{0.293,0,0.5117}\implies}\}`$,
and relations
$`\mathcal{B}_{r}=\{{\color[rgb]{0.293,0,0.5117}==},{\color[rgb]{0.293,0,0.5117}\leq},{\color[rgb]{0.293,0,0.5117}\geq},{\color[rgb]{0.293,0,0.5117}<},{\color[rgb]{0.293,0,0.5117}>}\}`$
with their usual semantics. We use a planner LLM
$`\mathcal{L}_{p}{}:\Sigma^{*}\to\Sigma^{*}`$ to search the program
space by sampling candidate programs as strings. We assume that
$`\mathcal{L}_{p}{}`$’s output space can represent all valid Dafny
programs $`L(G_{D})\subseteq\Sigma^{*}`$ and that the type
$`{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}string}`$ can represent all strings $`\Sigma^{*}`$
over $`\Sigma{}`$. SEVerA provides built-in predicates
$`{\color[rgb]{0.293,0,0.5117}lex_{T}}(x:{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}string})\to{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}bool}`$
to check whether a string can be parsed as a specific type
$`T\in\{{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}bool},{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}int},{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}real}\}`$.
Using Dafny as the language allows us to leverage its built-in verifier
to check candidate programs against a first-order input–output
specification, as well as its built-in termination checker. This choice
is motivated by several factors: (1) Dafny’s built-in verification
infrastructure directly supports the formal guarantees central to
SEVerA, (2) its type system aligns with the basic types $`\mathsf{T}`$
used in our specification language, and (3) it supports annotations such
as loop invariants and ranking functions that our planner LLM can
synthesize to aid the verifier. While the framework is not
language-specific, using a verification-aware host language avoids
re-implementing a custom verifier and termination checker.

Library Functions: We categorize the set of library functions
$`\mathcal{F}`$ into two disjoint sets: $`\mathcal{F}_{c}`$, the set of
non-parametric functions, and $`\mathcal{F}_{p}`$, the set of parametric
functions. $`\mathcal{F}_{c}`$ includes all built-in functions. Each
user specified non-parametric function of arity $`n`$ is specified by a
tuple
$`({\color[rgb]{0.293,0,0.5117}id(f_{n})},\tau_{f_{n}},{f_{n}}^{\Phi},{f_{n}}^{\Psi})`$,
where $`{\color[rgb]{0.293,0,0.5117}id(f_{n})}`$ is the function name,
$`\tau_{f_{n}}=(T_{1}\times\cdots\times T_{n}\to T_{0})`$ is the type
signature with $`T_{i}\in\mathsf{T}`$, and
$`({f_{n}}^{\Phi},{f_{n}}^{\Psi})`$ are first-order input–output
specifications defining a formal over-approximate semantics of
$`f_{n}`$. The function $`f_{n}:T_{1}\times\cdots\times T_{n}\to T_{0}`$
halts for any inputs $`x_{1}\in T_{1},\dots,x_{n}\in T_{n}`$ and
computes $`r=f_{n}(x_{1},\dots,x_{n})`$. The computed output $`r`$,
together with $`(x_{1},\dots,x_{n})`$, always satisfies
$`\forall x_{1}\in T_{1},\dots,\forall x_{n}\in T_{n}.\ {f_{n}}^{\Phi}(x_{1},\dots,x_{n})\implies{f_{n}}^{\Psi}(x_{1},\dots,x_{n},r)`$.
$`\mathcal{A}{}`$ contains all these formal contracts.

Parametric Functions: Each $`f^{\Theta{}}_{n}`$ in $`\mathcal{F}_{p}`$
is specified by the tuple
$`({\color[rgb]{0.293,0,0.5117}id(f^{\Theta{}}_{n})},\tau_{f^{\Theta{}}_{n}},\theta_{0},\Theta{})`$,
where $`{\color[rgb]{0.293,0,0.5117}id(f^{\Theta{}}_{n})}`$ denotes the
function name, $`\tau_{f^{\Theta{}}_{n}}`$ is the type signature,
$`\Theta{}`$ is a continuous set of parameters, and
$`\theta_{0}\in\Theta{}`$ denotes the default parameters. Here,
$`f^{\Theta{}}_{n}=\{f^{\theta}_{n}\mid\theta\in\Theta{}\}`$ represents
an infinite set of functions with the same type signature
$`\tau_{f^{\Theta{}}_{n}}`$, where each individual function
$`f^{\theta}_{n}\in f^{\Theta{}}_{n}`$ is instantiated by a concrete
parameter value $`\theta\in\Theta`$. Although $`f^{\Theta{}}_{n}`$
represents a set of functions, we sometimes abuse this notation to
denote a single function corresponding to $`f^{\theta_{0}}_{n}`$ with
the default parameters.

The input
$`\mathcal{I}=(\mathcal{F},\mathcal{A}{},\mathsf{L}{},\mathrm{D}{},\Phi,\Psi,I)`$
to SEVerA includes the library functions $`\mathcal{F}`$, axioms
$`\mathcal{A}{}`$, point-wise differentiable loss $`\mathsf{L}{}`$,
dataset $`\mathrm{D}`$, behavioral specifications $`(\Phi,\Psi)`$, and
textual task information $`I`$ used by the planner LLM
$`\mathcal{L}_{p}{}`$. We use
$`\mathcal{P}_{\mathsf{C}{}}:\Sigma^{*}\to\{T,F\}`$ to denote the parser
for checking the syntactic validity of input programs,
$`\mathcal{V}_{\mathsf{C}{}}[\Phi,\Psi]:\Sigma^{*}\to\{T,F\}`$ to denote
the verifier that checks a program against the specifications
$`(\Phi,\Psi)`$, and $`\mathcal{T}_{\mathsf{C}{}}:\Sigma^{*}\to\{T,F\}`$
to denote the termination checker. Each of
$`\mathcal{P}_{\mathsf{C}{}}`$,
$`\mathcal{V}_{\mathsf{C}{}}[\Phi,\Psi]`$, and
$`\mathcal{T}_{\mathsf{C}{}}`$ is instantiated with user-provided
context $`\mathsf{C}=(G_{D},\mathcal{F},\mathcal{A}{})`$. Both
$`\mathcal{V}_{\mathsf{C}{}}[\Phi,\Psi]`$ and
$`\mathcal{T}_{\mathsf{C}{}}{}`$ are restricted to a fixed timeout and
return false if they cannot verify $`(\Phi,\Psi)`$ or prove termination
within the allotted time budget.

### 5.2. Key Steps

#### 5.2.1. FGGM Formal Definition

Eq. [15](#S5.E15 "In 5.2.1. FGGM Formal Definition ‣ 5.2. Key Steps ‣ 5. Technical Details ‣ SEVerA: Verified Self-Evolving Agents")
specifies the formal syntax for defining an FGGM.

|  |  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|----|
| (15) |  | $`\displaystyle\langle{\color[rgb]{0.293,0,0.5117}FGGM}\rangle`$ | $`\displaystyle::=\langle{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}id}\rangle\ \text{";"}\ \langle{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}GMid}\rangle\text{";"}\ \overbrace{\langle{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}typeSig}\rangle\ \text{";"}\ \langle{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\Phi_{l}}\rangle\text{";"}\ \langle{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\Psi_{l}}\rangle\ \text{";"}}^{\text{signature + formal contract}}\underbrace{\langle{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}f_{p}}\rangle\text{";"}}_{\text{prompt}}\underbrace{\langle{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}f_{d}}\rangle\text{";"}}_{\text{fallback}}\langle{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}info}\rangle`$ |  |

The planner LLM defines a guarded GM following
Eq. [15](#S5.E15 "In 5.2.1. FGGM Formal Definition ‣ 5.2. Key Steps ‣ 5. Technical Details ‣ SEVerA: Verified Self-Evolving Agents"),
where: (a) id: is the unique identifier of the created FGGM; (b) GMid:
identifies the underlying GM used as the proposal distribution; (c)
typeSig: defines the type signature of the FGGM, including input
variables with their types and the output type, e.g.,
$`(x_{1}:{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}T_{1}},\dots,x_{n}:{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}T_{n}})\to{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}T_{o}}`$;
(d) $`(\Phi_{l},\Psi_{l})`$: are first-order formulas whose terms can
include non-parametric library functions from $`\mathcal{F}_{c}`$; (e)
$`f_{p}`$: is the program that constructs the GM input from the typed
input variables and the task description; (f) $`f_{d}`$: is a
non-parametric fallback program that satisfies the local specifications
$`(\Phi_{l},\Psi_{l})`$; and (g) info: is a textual description of the
defined FGGM, utilized by the planner LLM during the generation of the
parametric program. SEVerA parses these inputs, validates the
definition, and automatically synthesizes a rejection sampler with
fallback, as shown in
Fig. [2](#S4.F2 "Figure 2 ‣ 4.2.1. Intuition ‣ 4.2. Formally Guarded Generative Model ‣ 4. Overview ‣ SEVerA: Verified Self-Evolving Agents")
where $`\mathcal{L}_{\Theta}`$ is the parametric GM specified by GMid.
The defined FGGM is then invoked in the candidate program via its
identifier $`{\color[rgb]{0.293,0,0.5117}id}`$. For valid definitions,
SEVerA synthesizes
$`{\color[rgb]{0.293,0,0.5117}check_{\mathcal{A},\Phi_{l},\Psi_{l}}}`$,
which checks whether a concrete input–output pair
$`(x_{1},\dots,x_{n},y)`$ satisfies the proposed contract
$`(\Phi_{l},\Psi_{l})`$, as elaborated in
§ [5.2.3](#S5.SS2.SSS3 "5.2.3. Computability of 𝑐⁢ℎ⁢𝑒⁢𝑐⁢𝑘_{𝒜,Φ_𝑙,Ψ_𝑙} (Fig. ) on concrete values ‣ 5.2. Key Steps ‣ 5. Technical Details ‣ SEVerA: Verified Self-Evolving Agents").

We provide the BNF grammar for parsing the FGGM definition in
Appendix [L](#A12 "Appendix L FGGM Syntax ‣ SEVerA: Verified Self-Evolving Agents").
Next, we discuss correctness checks for a proposed FGGM definition.
Provided the SEVerA validates definition including the fallback
$`f_{d}`$,
$`\forall\theta\in\Theta.\forall x_{1}\in T_{1}\dots\forall x_{n}\in T_{n}.\Phi_{l}(x_{1},\dots,x_{n})\implies\Psi_{l}(x_{1},\dots,x_{n},{\color[rgb]{0.293,0,0.5117}id}(x_{1},\dots,x_{n}))`$
holds ensuring formal contracts are preserved for all parametric values
$`\theta\in\Theta`$.

#### 5.2.2. FGGM Well-formedness

Given an FGGM definition
$`\mathsf{G}{}=({\color[rgb]{0.293,0,0.5117}id_{\mathsf{G}}},f^{\Theta{}}_{\mathsf{G}{}},\tau_{\mathsf{G}{}},\Phi_{l},\Psi_{l},f_{p},f_{d},info)`$
following
Eq. [15](#S5.E15 "In 5.2.1. FGGM Formal Definition ‣ 5.2. Key Steps ‣ 5. Technical Details ‣ SEVerA: Verified Self-Evolving Agents"),
this step checks whether the definition is well-formed. Let the
parametric GM identified by GMid be
$`\mathcal{L}_{\Theta}:T_{in}\rightarrow T_{o}`$. SEVerA first checks
the well-formedness of the type signature
$`\tau_{\mathsf{G}{}}=(T_{1}\times\cdots\times T_{n})\to T_{o}`$ and the
well-formedness of the local contracts $`(\Phi_{l},\Psi_{l})`$. We then
verify that all terms in $`\Phi_{l}`$ and subsequently in $`\Psi_{l}`$
that involve non-parametric functions from $`\mathcal{F}_{c}`$ are valid
(details in
Appendix [M](#A13 "Appendix M FGGM Validity Check ‣ SEVerA: Verified Self-Evolving Agents")).
The $`\mathsf{G}{}`$ definition is considered valid provided both
$`f_{p}`$ and $`f_{d}`$ are type-checked and terminating, and the
fallback $`f_{d}`$ satisfies the contract
$`\mathcal{V}_{\mathsf{C}{}}[\Phi_{l},\Psi_{l}](f_{d})`$. After the
validity check, SEVerA constructs
$`{\color[rgb]{0.293,0,0.5117}check_{\mathcal{A},\Phi_{l},\Psi_{l}}}:(T_{1}\times\cdots\times T_{n}\times T_{o})\to\{T,F\}`$
that checks whether a concrete input–output tuple
$`(x_{1},\dots,x_{n},y)`$ satisfies the local output contract
$`\Psi_{l}`$ (see
§ [5.2.3](#S5.SS2.SSS3 "5.2.3. Computability of 𝑐⁢ℎ⁢𝑒⁢𝑐⁢𝑘_{𝒜,Φ_𝑙,Ψ_𝑙} (Fig. ) on concrete values ‣ 5.2. Key Steps ‣ 5. Technical Details ‣ SEVerA: Verified Self-Evolving Agents")).
We provide the pseudocode of
$`{\color[rgb]{0.293,0,0.5117}check_{\mathcal{A},\Phi_{l},\Psi_{l}}}`$
along with a soundness proof showing
$`\varphi_{\mathcal{A}{}}\implies\big(\forall x_{1}\in T_{1},\dots,\forall x_{n}\in T_{n},\forall y\in T_{o}.\;\Phi_{l}(x_{1},\dots,x_{n})\implies\left({\color[rgb]{0.293,0,0.5117}check_{\mathcal{A},\Phi_{l},\Psi_{l}}}(x_{1},\dots,x_{n},y)\implies\Psi_{l}(x_{1},\dots,x_{n},y)\right)\big)`$
in
Appendix [R](#A18 "Appendix R Proof Details ‣ SEVerA: Verified Self-Evolving Agents").
Furthermore, for quantifier-free $`\Psi_{l}`$, the checker is complete
(Lemma [5.1](#S5.Thmtheorem1 "Lemma 5.1 (Completeness of Checker). ‣ 5.2.2. FGGM Well-formedness ‣ 5.2. Key Steps ‣ 5. Technical Details ‣ SEVerA: Verified Self-Evolving Agents")).

###### Lemma 5.1 (Completeness of Checker).

For any valid FGGM $`\mathsf{G}{}`$ with quantifier-free $`\Psi_{l}`$,
$`\forall x_{1}\in T_{1},\dots,\forall x_{n}\in T_{n},\forall y\in T_{o}.\;\Phi_{l}(x_{1},\dots,x_{n})\implies\left({\color[rgb]{0.293,0,0.5117}check_{\mathcal{A},\Phi_{l},\Psi_{l}}}(x_{1},\dots,x_{n},y)\iff\Psi_{l}(x_{1},\dots,x_{n},y)\right)`$.

###### Proof Sketch.

We prove this by structural induction on the quantifier-free formula
$`\Psi_{l}`$. *Base case:* If $`\Psi_{l}`$ is an atomic predicate over
terms built from computable library functions in $`\mathcal{F}_{c}`$,
then under any concrete substitution $`(x_{1},\dots,x_{n},y)`$,
$`{\color[rgb]{0.293,0,0.5117}check_{\mathcal{A},\Phi_{l},\Psi_{l}}}`$
evaluates the same computable terms and returns the same boolean value
as $`\Psi_{l}`$. *Inductive step:* Assume the claim holds for formulas
$`\phi`$ and $`\psi`$. For compound formulas $`\neg\phi`$,
$`\phi\wedge\psi`$, and $`\phi\vee\psi`$,
$`{\color[rgb]{0.293,0,0.5117}check_{\mathcal{A},\Phi_{l},\Psi_{l}}}`$
recursively evaluates the subformulas and applies the corresponding
boolean operator, and returns the result. Thus, by induction on the
structure of $`\Psi_{l}`$,
$`{\color[rgb]{0.293,0,0.5117}check_{\mathcal{A},\Phi_{l},\Psi_{l}}}(x_{1},\dots,x_{n},y)`$
returns true iff $`\Psi_{l}(x_{1},\dots,x_{n},y)`$ holds whenever
$`\Phi_{l}(x_{1},\dots,x_{n})`$ holds. Hence, the checker is complete.
Formal details in
Appendix [R](#A18 "Appendix R Proof Details ‣ SEVerA: Verified Self-Evolving Agents").
∎

For any valid FGGM $`\mathsf{G}{}`$, the rejection sampler
$`{\color[rgb]{0.293,0,0.5117}id_{\mathsf{G}{}}}:T_{1}\times\cdots\times T_{n}\to T_{o}`$
with fallback synthesized by SEVerA
(Fig. [2](#S4.F2 "Figure 2 ‣ 4.2.1. Intuition ‣ 4.2. Formally Guarded Generative Model ‣ 4. Overview ‣ SEVerA: Verified Self-Evolving Agents"))
satisfies the defined contract $`(\Phi_{l},\Psi_{l})`$ for all
well-typed inputs $`(x_{1},\dots,x_{n})`$. Crucially the contract
preservation holds over all parameters $`\theta\in\Theta`$ of the
underlying parametric model $`f^{\Theta{}}_{\mathsf{G}{}}`$. The
function $`{\color[rgb]{0.293,0,0.5117}id_{\mathsf{G}{}}}`$ terminates
on all inputs since the number of samples $`K`$ is finite and $`f_{p}`$,
$`f_{d}`$, and
$`{\color[rgb]{0.293,0,0.5117}check_{\mathcal{A},\Phi_{l},\Psi_{l}}}`$
are all terminating. We provide a soundness proof sketch in
Theorem [5.2](#S5.Thmtheorem2 "Theorem 5.2 (Valid Local contract). ‣ 5.2.2. FGGM Well-formedness ‣ 5.2. Key Steps ‣ 5. Technical Details ‣ SEVerA: Verified Self-Evolving Agents").

###### Theorem 5.2 (Valid Local contract).

For any valid FGGM $`\mathsf{G}{}`$ with $`(\Phi_{l},\Psi_{l})`$ and
parametric GM $`f^{\Theta{}}_{\mathsf{G}{}}`$,
$`\varphi_{\mathcal{A}{}}\implies\big(\forall\theta\in\Theta,\forall x_{1}\in T_{1},\dots,\forall x_{n}\in T_{n}.\;\Phi_{l}(x_{1},\dots,x_{n})\implies\Psi_{l}(x_{1},\dots,x_{n},{\color[rgb]{0.293,0,0.5117}id_{\mathsf{G}{}}}(x_{1},\dots,x_{n}))\big)`$.

###### Proof Sketch.

Let
$`r={\color[rgb]{0.293,0,0.5117}id_{\mathsf{G}{}}}(x_{1},\dots,x_{n})`$.
Based on the rejection sampler with the checker
$`{\color[rgb]{0.293,0,0.5117}check_{\mathcal{A},\Phi_{l},\Psi_{l}}}`$,
the following condition always holds for the output $`r`$
(Eq. [16](#S5.E16 "In Proof Sketch. ‣ 5.2.2. FGGM Well-formedness ‣ 5.2. Key Steps ‣ 5. Technical Details ‣ SEVerA: Verified Self-Evolving Agents")).
Eq. [17](#S5.E17 "In Proof Sketch. ‣ 5.2.2. FGGM Well-formedness ‣ 5.2. Key Steps ‣ 5. Technical Details ‣ SEVerA: Verified Self-Evolving Agents")
follows from the validity of the fallback $`f_{d}`$, and
Eq. [18](#S5.E18 "In Proof Sketch. ‣ 5.2.2. FGGM Well-formedness ‣ 5.2. Key Steps ‣ 5. Technical Details ‣ SEVerA: Verified Self-Evolving Agents")
follows from the soundness of the checker
$`{\color[rgb]{0.293,0,0.5117}check_{\mathcal{A},\Phi_{l},\Psi_{l}}}`$.
To simplify the notation, we used $`(\forall x_{i}\in T_{i})`$ to denote
$`(\forall x_{1}\in T_{1},\dots,\forall x_{n}\in T_{n})`$ and $`y_{f}`$
is the final rejected sample if $`f_{d}`$ is used.

|  |  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|----|
| (16) |  |  | $`\displaystyle\varphi_{\mathcal{A}{}}\implies(\forall\theta\in\Theta.(\forall x_{i}\in T_{i}).\Phi_{l}(x_{1},\dots,x_{n})\implies{\color[rgb]{0.293,0,0.5117}check_{\mathcal{A},\Phi_{l},\Psi_{l}}}(x_{1},\dots,x_{n},r)\vee(r=f_{d}(x_{1},\dots,x_{n},y_{f}))`$ |  |
| (17) |  |  | $`\displaystyle\varphi_{\mathcal{A}{}}\implies\forall\theta\in\Theta.(\forall x_{i}\in T_{i}).\Phi_{l}(x_{1},\dots,x_{n})\wedge(r=f_{d}(x_{1},\dots,x_{n},y_{f}))\implies\Psi_{l}(x_{1},\dots,x_{n},r)`$ |  |
| (18) |  |  | $`\displaystyle\varphi_{\mathcal{A}{}}\implies(\forall\theta\in\Theta.(\forall x_{i}\in T_{i}).(\Phi_{l}(x_{1},\dots,x_{n})\wedge{\color[rgb]{0.293,0,0.5117}check_{\mathcal{A},\Phi_{l},\Psi_{l}}}(x_{1},\dots,x_{n},r))\implies\Psi_{l}(x_{1},\dots,x_{n},r))`$ |  |
|  |  | $`\displaystyle\varphi_{\mathcal{A}{}}\implies(\forall\theta\in\Theta.(\forall x_{i}\in T_{i}).\Phi_{l}(x_{1},\dots,x_{n})\implies\Psi_{l}(x_{1},\dots,x_{n},r))\;\;\;\;\text{ Using Eq.~{(\ref{eq:FGGMsound1}, \ref{eq:FGGMsound2}, \ref{eq:FGGMsound3}}})`$ |  |  |

We provide the detailed formal proof in
Appendix [R](#A18 "Appendix R Proof Details ‣ SEVerA: Verified Self-Evolving Agents").
∎

#### 5.2.3. Computability of $`{\color[rgb]{0.293,0,0.5117}check_{\mathcal{A},\Phi_{l},\Psi_{l}}}`$ (Fig. [2](#S4.F2 "Figure 2 ‣ 4.2.1. Intuition ‣ 4.2. Formally Guarded Generative Model ‣ 4. Overview ‣ SEVerA: Verified Self-Evolving Agents")) on concrete values

The auto-synthesized rejection sampler
(Fig. [2](#S4.F2 "Figure 2 ‣ 4.2.1. Intuition ‣ 4.2. Formally Guarded Generative Model ‣ 4. Overview ‣ SEVerA: Verified Self-Evolving Agents"))
requires checking whether a sample $`y`$ from $`\mathcal{L}_{\Theta}`$,
given a concrete input $`(x_{1},\dots,x_{n})`$, satisfies the planner
LLM–defined $`\Psi_{l}`$. We show that for any quantifier-free
$`\Psi_{l}`$, this check can be computed efficiently for all concrete
values $`(x_{1},\dots,x_{n},y)`$. Since all library functions in
$`\mathcal{F}_{c}`$ are computable,
$`{\color[rgb]{0.293,0,0.5117}check_{\mathcal{A},\Phi_{l},\Psi_{l}}}`$
can evaluate every term on the concrete inputs
$`(x_{1},\dots,x_{n},y)`$. Satisfiability can then be decided in linear
time in the number of terms in $`\Psi_{l}`$. We provide formal
completeness for the quantifier-free fragment in
Lemma [5.1](#S5.Thmtheorem1 "Lemma 5.1 (Completeness of Checker). ‣ 5.2.2. FGGM Well-formedness ‣ 5.2. Key Steps ‣ 5. Technical Details ‣ SEVerA: Verified Self-Evolving Agents").
For $`\Psi_{l}`$ with quantifiers, we instantiate
$`{\color[rgb]{0.293,0,0.5117}check_{\mathcal{A},\Phi_{l},\Psi_{l}}}`$
with the axioms $`\mathcal{A}`$. Then,
$`{\color[rgb]{0.293,0,0.5117}check_{\mathcal{A},\Phi_{l},\Psi_{l}}}`$
substitutes the free variables in $`\Psi_{l}`$ with their corresponding
concrete values, encodes the axioms $`\mathcal{A}`$ and $`\Phi_{l}`$
similarly to
Eq. [8](#S4.E8 "In 4.1.1. Constrained Symbolic Regression: ‣ 4.1. Example Instantiation of SEVerA ‣ 4. Overview ‣ SEVerA: Verified Self-Evolving Agents"),
and submits the resulting formula to an SMT solver. First-order formulas
over the basic types $`\mathsf{T}`$ and uninterpreted library functions
may lie outside decidable fragments. Therefore, we bound the SMT solver
with a user-specified timeout.
$`{\color[rgb]{0.293,0,0.5117}check_{\mathcal{A},\Phi_{l},\Psi_{l}}}`$
returns true only if the solver succeeds within the timeout; otherwise,
it returns false. This guarantees soundness; however, in the presence of
quantifiers,
$`{\color[rgb]{0.293,0,0.5117}check_{\mathcal{A},\Phi_{l},\Psi_{l}}}`$
may be incomplete and may incorrectly reject valid samples $`y`$.

1: Input: $`\mathcal{I}=(\mathcal{F},\mathcal{A}{},\Phi,\Psi,I)`$,
planner $`\mathcal{L}_{p}{}`$, budget $`\delta`$

2: Input: Previous attempts feed-back $`I^{\prime}`$

3: Output: Verified Parametric Program $`\mathsf{P}_{\{\Theta{}\}{}}{}`$
else $`\bot`$

4: $`i\leftarrow 0`$, $`\mathsf{err}\leftarrow\{\}`$

5: while $`i<\delta`$ do

6:
   $`\mathcal{G}\leftarrow{\color[rgb]{0.293,0,0.5117}defineFGGM}(\mathcal{L}_{p}{},I,\mathcal{F},\mathcal{A}{},I^{\prime},\mathsf{err})`$

7:
   $`\mathsf{err}\leftarrow{\color[rgb]{0.293,0,0.5117}validateFGGM}(\mathcal{G}{},\mathcal{F}_{c},\mathcal{A}{})`$

8:    if $`\mathsf{err}\neq\{\}`$ then

9:     $`i\leftarrow i+1`$;  continue

10:    end if

11:
   $`\mathsf{P}_{\{\Theta{}\}{}}{}\leftarrow{\color[rgb]{0.293,0,0.5117}sampleProgram}(\mathcal{L}_{p}{},I,\mathcal{F},\mathcal{A}{},I^{\prime},\mathcal{G}{},\mathsf{err})`$

12:
   $`\mathsf{C}\leftarrow(G_{D},\mathcal{F}\cup\mathcal{G}{},\mathcal{A}{}\cup\mathcal{A}{}_{\mathcal{G}{}})`$

13:
   $`\mathsf{err}\leftarrow{\color[rgb]{0.293,0,0.5117}validateProgram}(\mathsf{P}_{\{\Theta{}\}{}}{},\mathcal{P}_{\mathsf{C}{}}{},\mathcal{T}_{\mathsf{C}{}}{},\mathcal{V}_{\mathsf{C}{}}[\Phi,\Psi])`$

14:    if $`\mathsf{err}=\{\}`$ then

15:     return $`\mathsf{P}_{\{\Theta{}\}{}}{}`$

16:    end if

17:    $`i\leftarrow i+1`$

18: end while

19: return $`\bot`$

Algorithm 1 searchVerify

#### 5.2.4. Search and Verify

The search and verification steps jointly implement a CEGIS-style loop
that explores candidate parametric programs while enforcing the
behavioral specification. In the search phase, the planner LLM
$`\mathcal{L}_{p}{}`$ first synthesizes a set of FGGM definitions
$`\mathcal{G}=\{\mathsf{G}{}_{1},\dots,\mathsf{G}{}_{m}\}`$ following
Eq. [15](#S5.E15 "In 5.2.1. FGGM Formal Definition ‣ 5.2. Key Steps ‣ 5. Technical Details ‣ SEVerA: Verified Self-Evolving Agents").
Each FGGM wraps a parametric model with local contracts and a verified
fallback. Using these FGGMs as callable functions, the planner then
samples a candidate parametric program $`\mathsf{P}_{\{\Theta{}\}{}}{}`$
where $`\{\Theta{}\}{}=\{\Theta{}_{1},\dots,\Theta{}_{k}\}`$ represents
the set of all optimizable parameters in
$`\mathsf{P}_{\{\Theta{}\}{}}{}`$. As mentioned in
§ [4.3.1](#S4.SS3.SSS1 "4.3.1. Candidate Pool and Execution Feedback ‣ 4.3. SEVerA ‣ 4. Overview ‣ SEVerA: Verified Self-Evolving Agents"),
FGGM calls at different program locations do not share parameters and
add their own parameter in $`\{\Theta{}\}{}`$. In the verification
phase, SEVerA first checks the well-formedness of every
$`\mathsf{G}{}_{i}\in\mathcal{G}`$. If any of the definitions fail to
verify it returns an error message. If all definitions are valid, the
verification context $`\mathsf{C}=(G_{D},\mathcal{F},\mathcal{A}{})`$ is
extended with the synthesized FGGMs and their local contracts. The
updated context
$`\mathsf{C}^{\prime}=(G_{D},\mathcal{F}\cup\mathcal{G}{},\mathcal{A}{}\cup\mathcal{A}_{\mathcal{G}{}})`$
adds all FGGMs $`\mathcal{G}{}`$ along with
$`\mathcal{A}_{\mathcal{G}{}}`$ containing local contracts
$`(\mathsf{G}{}_{i}^{\Phi_{l}},\mathsf{G}{}_{i}^{\Psi_{l}})`$ of each
FGGM $`\mathsf{G}{}_{i}\in\mathcal{G}{}`$. The candidate program
$`\mathsf{P}_{\{\Theta{}\}{}}{}`$ is then checked for syntactic
validity, termination, and compliance with the behavioral specification
$`(\Phi,\Psi)`$. If verification succeeds, SEVerA accepts the parametric
program $`\mathsf{P}_{\{\Theta{}\}{}}{}`$ and ensures that
$`\mathsf{P}_{\{\Theta{}\}{}}{}`$ satisfies $`(\Phi,\Psi)`$ over all
parameters
(Theorem [5.3](#S5.Thmtheorem3 "Theorem 5.3. ‣ 5.2.4. Search and Verify ‣ 5.2. Key Steps ‣ 5. Technical Details ‣ SEVerA: Verified Self-Evolving Agents")).
Algorithm [1](#alg1 "Algorithm 1 ‣ 5.2.3. Computability of 𝑐⁢ℎ⁢𝑒⁢𝑐⁢𝑘_{𝒜,Φ_𝑙,Ψ_𝑙} (Fig. ) on concrete values ‣ 5.2. Key Steps ‣ 5. Technical Details ‣ SEVerA: Verified Self-Evolving Agents")
summarizes the combined search–verification loop.

Given the input specification $`\mathcal{I}`$ and planner
$`\mathcal{L}_{p}{}`$, the algorithm iteratively proposes candidate
solutions within a fixed budget $`\delta`$ (Lines 1–4). In each
iteration, the planner first synthesizes a set of FGGM definitions
$`\mathcal{G}`$ (Line 6), which are then checked for well-formedness
using $`{\color[rgb]{0.293,0,0.5117}validateFGGM}`$ (Line 7). Within
$`\mathcal{G}`$, the planner LLM $`\mathcal{L}_{p}{}`$ also synthesizes
the prompting functions $`f_{p}{}`$, enabling each FGGM-specific
customization. If the definitions are valid, the planner samples a
candidate parametric program $`\mathsf{P}_{\{\Theta{}\}{}}{}`$ that may
invoke these FGGMs (Line 11), and the verification context is extended
with their contracts (Line 12). The candidate program is then validated
for syntactic correctness, termination, and compliance with the
behavioral specification using
$`{\color[rgb]{0.293,0,0.5117}validateProgram}`$ (Line 13). If
verification succeeds, the program is returned (Lines 14–15); otherwise,
the loop continues with the error feedback until the search budget is
exhausted (Lines 16–18).

###### Theorem 5.3.

If $`\;\mathsf{P}_{\{\Theta{}\}{}}{}\neq\bot`$ with FGGM set
$`\mathcal{G}{}`$, then
$`\forall\theta_{1}\in\Theta_{1},\dots,\forall\theta_{k}\in\Theta_{k}.\varphi_{\mathcal{A}{}}\implies\big(\forall x_{1}\in T_{1},\dots,\forall x_{n}\in T_{n}.\Phi(x_{1},\dots,x_{n})\implies\Psi(x_{1},\dots,x_{n},\mathsf{P}_{\{(\theta_{1},\dots,\theta_{k})/\Theta\}}(x_{1},\dots,x_{n}))\big)`$.

###### Proof Sketch.

Follows from
Theorem [5.2](#S5.Thmtheorem2 "Theorem 5.2 (Valid Local contract). ‣ 5.2.2. FGGM Well-formedness ‣ 5.2. Key Steps ‣ 5. Technical Details ‣ SEVerA: Verified Self-Evolving Agents")
with details in
Appendix [R](#A18 "Appendix R Proof Details ‣ SEVerA: Verified Self-Evolving Agents").
∎

#### 5.2.5. Learn

Once a candidate parametric program $`\mathsf{P}_{\{\Theta{}\}{}}{}`$
passes the search–verification loop
(Algorithm [1](#alg1 "Algorithm 1 ‣ 5.2.3. Computability of 𝑐⁢ℎ⁢𝑒⁢𝑐⁢𝑘_{𝒜,Φ_𝑙,Ψ_𝑙} (Fig. ) on concrete values ‣ 5.2. Key Steps ‣ 5. Technical Details ‣ SEVerA: Verified Self-Evolving Agents")),
the verification step guarantees that $`\mathsf{P}_{\{\Theta{}\}{}}{}`$
satisfies the behavioral specification $`(\Phi,\Psi)`$ for *all*
parameter values
(Theorem [5.3](#S5.Thmtheorem3 "Theorem 5.3. ‣ 5.2.4. Search and Verify ‣ 5.2. Key Steps ‣ 5. Technical Details ‣ SEVerA: Verified Self-Evolving Agents")).
Hence, the learning step can freely select parameters without violating
$`(\Phi,\Psi)`$. Finding the optimal solution to the general formulation
in
Eq. [19](#S5.E19 "In 5.2.5. Learn ‣ 5.2. Key Steps ‣ 5. Technical Details ‣ SEVerA: Verified Self-Evolving Agents")
over $`\{\Theta{}\}{}`$ for a general loss $`\mathsf{L}{}`$ is
practically intractable. Instead, SEVerA employs a scalable
gradient-descent–based optimization to efficiently search over
$`\{\Theta{}\}{}`$.

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
| (19) |  | $`\displaystyle({\theta_{1}}^{*},\dots,{\theta_{k}}^{*})=\argmin_{(\theta_{1},\dots,\theta_{k})\in\{\Theta{}\}{}}\;\;{\textstyle\sum_{(x,y)\in\mathrm{D}}\mathsf{L}{}(x,y,\mathsf{P}_{\{(\theta_{1},\dots,\theta_{k})/\Theta\}}(x))}`$ |  |

Conformance loss $`\mathsf{L}_{\Phi_{l},\Psi_{l}}{}`$ for each local
contract $`(\Phi_{l},\Psi_{l})`$ encourages the parameters to produce
outputs that satisfy their local contracts. By improving conformance
with these contracts, SEVerA increases the success rate of the
corresponding rejection sampler and thereby avoids triggering the static
non-parametric fallback program. Since the fallback cannot be tuned,
reducing its usage allows the gradient-based search to more effectively
guide the parameters toward solutions that reduce the final loss
$`\mathsf{L}{}`$. Our experiments in
§ [6.3](#S6.SS3 "6.3. Constraint Decomposition ‣ 6. Evaluation ‣ SEVerA: Verified Self-Evolving Agents")
substantiate this observation, showing that reducing reliance on the
fallback improves task performance. For a single FGGM with local
contracts $`(\Phi_{l},\Psi_{l})`$ and parameter $`\theta`$, we define
the conformance loss over an input set $`\mathbb{P}`$ in
Eq. [20](#S5.E20 "In 5.2.5. Learn ‣ 5.2. Key Steps ‣ 5. Technical Details ‣ SEVerA: Verified Self-Evolving Agents").
The inner term $`\mathsf{L}_{\Phi_{l},\Psi_{l}}^{\theta}(p)`$ measures
the probability that a sampled output from $`\mathcal{L}_{\theta}(p)`$
violates
$`{\color[rgb]{0.293,0,0.5117}check_{\mathcal{A},\Phi_{l},\Psi_{l}}}`$,
while $`\mathsf{L}_{\Phi_{l},\Psi_{l}}(\theta)`$ aggregates this
violation across inputs.

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
| (20) |  | $`\displaystyle\underbrace{\mathsf{L}_{\Phi_{l},\Psi_{l}}(\theta)=\tfrac{1}{|\mathbb{P}|}\times{\textstyle\sum_{p\in\mathbb{P}}\mathsf{L}_{\Phi_{l},\Psi_{l}}^{\theta}(p)}}_{\text{Aggregated constraint violation over $\mathbb{P}$}},\;\;\text{ where }\mathsf{L}_{\Phi_{l},\Psi_{l}}^{\theta}(p)=\underbrace{\mathbb{E}_{y\sim\mathcal{L}_{\theta}(p)}1-\mathbb{I}({\color[rgb]{0.293,0,0.5117}check_{\mathcal{A},\Phi_{l},\Psi_{l}}}(x_{1},\dots,x_{n},y))}_{\text{Expected constraint violation on single GM input $p$}}`$ |  |

The augmented objective, which includes a local conformance loss for
each FGGM call, is defined in
Eq. [21](#S5.E21 "In 5.2.5. Learn ‣ 5.2. Key Steps ‣ 5. Technical Details ‣ SEVerA: Verified Self-Evolving Agents"),
where $`\lambda\in\mathbb{R}^{+}`$ is a user-provided constant.

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
| (21) |  | $`\displaystyle{\textstyle\sum_{(x,y)\in\mathrm{D}}\mathsf{L}{}(x,y,\mathsf{P}_{\{(\theta_{1},\dots,\theta_{k})/\Theta\}}(x))}\;+\;\lambda\times{\textstyle\sum_{i\in k,(x,y)\in\mathrm{D}}\mathsf{L}{}^{i}_{\Phi_{l},\Psi_{l}}(\theta_{i})}`$ |  |

Here, the first term is the task-specific loss over the dataset
$`\mathrm{D}`$, and the second term aggregates the local conformance
losses
(Eq. [20](#S5.E20 "In 5.2.5. Learn ‣ 5.2. Key Steps ‣ 5. Technical Details ‣ SEVerA: Verified Self-Evolving Agents"))
of the FGGMs appearing in the program. Optimizing all parameters jointly
according to
Eq. [21](#S5.E21 "In 5.2.5. Learn ‣ 5.2. Key Steps ‣ 5. Technical Details ‣ SEVerA: Verified Self-Evolving Agents"),
while feasible for smaller neural networks, becomes practically
expensive for agents with multiple interdependent LLM calls. To address
this challenge, we leverage a key structural property: the conformance
loss $`\mathsf{L}{}^{i}_{\Phi_{l},\Psi_{l}}(\theta_{i})`$ for each FGGM
depends only on the local inputs to that FGGM call and the outputs of
its underlying GM, not on the parameters of other FGGMs. This
independence arises because each FGGM’s rejection sampler and
$`{\color[rgb]{0.293,0,0.5117}check_{\mathcal{A},\Phi_{l},\Psi_{l}}}`$
checker operate solely on the local contract
$`(\Phi_{l}^{i},\Psi_{l}^{i})`$ and the corresponding GM’s outputs. As a
result, the conformance term decomposes naturally across FGGM calls.
Following this observation, for larger models we approximate the
augmented loss by optimizing each FGGM
$`{\color[rgb]{0.293,0,0.5117}id_{\theta_{i}}}`$ with parameter
$`\theta_{i}`$ independently, as shown in
Eq. [22](#S5.E22 "In 5.2.5. Learn ‣ 5.2. Key Steps ‣ 5. Technical Details ‣ SEVerA: Verified Self-Evolving Agents").
Here, the first term includes the task-specific loss $`\mathsf{L}{}`$
only when the output $`y_{l}`$ of
$`{\color[rgb]{0.293,0,0.5117}id_{\theta_{i}}}`$ matches the final
output $`y`$ of the agent on input $`x`$, where $`(x,\_)\in\mathrm{D}`$.
The modularized loss
(Eq. [22](#S5.E22 "In 5.2.5. Learn ‣ 5.2. Key Steps ‣ 5. Technical Details ‣ SEVerA: Verified Self-Evolving Agents"))
enables efficient parallelized training across different $`\theta_{i}`$.

|  |  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|----|
| (22) |  |  | $`\displaystyle\mathsf{L}{}_{a}(\theta_{i})=\tfrac{1}{|\mathbb{P}|}\times{\textstyle\sum_{p\in\mathbb{P}}\mathsf{L}{}_{a}^{\theta_{i}}(p)};\;\;\;\;\mathsf{L}{}^{\theta_{i}}_{a}(p)=\mathbb{E}_{y_{l}\sim{\color[rgb]{0.293,0,0.5117}id_{\theta_{i}}}(p)}\mathsf{L}{}(x,\_,y)\times\mathbb{I}(y=y_{l})+\lambda\times\mathsf{L}_{\Phi_{l},\Psi_{l}}^{\theta_{i}}(p)`$ |  |
| (23) |  |  | $`\displaystyle\mathcal{R}(p,y_{l})=1-{\color[rgb]{0.293,0,0.5117}Sigmoid}\big(\mathsf{L}{}(x,\_,y)\times\mathbb{I}(y=y_{l})+\lambda\times(1-\mathbb{I}({\color[rgb]{0.293,0,0.5117}check_{\mathcal{A},\Phi_{l},\Psi_{l}}}(p,y_{l}))\big)`$ |  |

For generative models with accessible parameters, the objective in
Eq. [22](#S5.E22 "In 5.2.5. Learn ‣ 5.2. Key Steps ‣ 5. Technical Details ‣ SEVerA: Verified Self-Evolving Agents")
can be optimized using reinforcement learning–based fine-tuning methods
such as GRPO ([Shao et al., 2024](#bib.bib22)) (details in
Appendix [N](#A14 "Appendix N Background on GRPO ‣ SEVerA: Verified Self-Evolving Agents")).
Eq. [23](#S5.E23 "In 5.2.5. Learn ‣ 5.2. Key Steps ‣ 5. Technical Details ‣ SEVerA: Verified Self-Evolving Agents")
defines the reward for an input-output pair $`(p,y_{l})`$, with the goal
of learning an output distribution over $`y_{l}`$ for inputs
$`p\in\mathbb{P}`$ that maximizes total reward $`\mathcal{R}(p,y_{l})`$.
The reward function combines two signals: (1) the task-specific loss
$`\mathsf{L}{}`$, which drives the GM toward outputs that reduce overall
task error, and (2) the conformance indicator
$`\mathbb{I}({\color[rgb]{0.293,0,0.5117}check_{\mathcal{A},\Phi_{l},\Psi_{l}}}(p,y_{l}))`$,
which rewards outputs satisfying the local contract. The sigmoid
transformation maps the combined penalty to the $`[0,1]`$ range,
providing a smooth reward landscape. Outputs that violate the local
contract receive near-zero reward due to the
$`(1-\mathbb{I}({\color[rgb]{0.293,0,0.5117}check_{\mathcal{A},\Phi_{l},\Psi_{l}}}(p,y_{l})))`$
penalty term, strongly discouraging the GM from producing outputs that
would be rejected by the rejection sampler. The reward function need not
be differentiable w.r.t. $`\theta_{i}`$, as long as the outputs
$`y_{l}`$ remain differentiable w.r.t. $`\theta_{i}`$ ([Shao et al.,
2024](#bib.bib22)). For closed-source models with inaccessible
parameters, the learning step is skipped, and performance improvements
rely solely on prompt tuning through the synthesized $`f_{p}`$ programs
within each FGGM.

#### 5.2.6. SEVerA

Algorithm [2](#alg2 "Algorithm 2 ‣ 5.2.6. SEVerA ‣ 5.2. Key Steps ‣ 5. Technical Details ‣ SEVerA: Verified Self-Evolving Agents")
summarizes the overall workflow of SEVerA. The algorithm maintains a
pool $`\mathcal{P}`$ of verified candidate agents and iteratively
improves it through a search–verify–learn loop. In each iteration,
SEVerA first invokes the searchVerify procedure
(Algorithm [1](#alg1 "Algorithm 1 ‣ 5.2.3. Computability of 𝑐⁢ℎ⁢𝑒⁢𝑐⁢𝑘_{𝒜,Φ_𝑙,Ψ_𝑙} (Fig. ) on concrete values ‣ 5.2. Key Steps ‣ 5. Technical Details ‣ SEVerA: Verified Self-Evolving Agents")),
which performs CEGIS-style discrete search to synthesize FGGM
definitions and candidate parametric program
$`\mathsf{P}_{\{\Theta{}\}{}}{}`$ that satisfy the behavioral
specification $`(\Phi,\Psi)`$. If verification succeeds, the program is
passed to the learn procedure, which optimizes the parameters of the
underlying generative models using the dataset $`\mathrm{D}`$ and task
loss $`\mathsf{L}{}`$. For closed-source models with inaccessible
parameters, this step is skipped, and performance improvements rely
solely on prompt tuning through the synthesized $`f_{p}`$ programs in
each FGGM.

1: Input:
$`\mathcal{I}=(\mathcal{F},\mathcal{A}{},\mathsf{L}{},\mathrm{D}{},\Phi,\Psi,I)`$,
planner $`\mathcal{L}_{p}{}`$

2: Input: total budget $`\Delta`$, budget per candidate $`\delta`$

3: Output: Best agent $`{f}^{*}`$ or $`\bot`$ if search fails

4: $`\mathcal{P}\leftarrow\{\}`$ $`\triangleright`$ Pool of verified
candidates

5: $`I^{\prime}\leftarrow\emptyset`$

6: while $`\delta\leq\Delta`$ do

7:
   $`\mathsf{P}_{\{\Theta{}\}{}}{}\leftarrow{\color[rgb]{0.293,0,0.5117}searchVerify}(\mathcal{F},\mathcal{A}{},\Phi,\Psi,I,\mathcal{L}_{p}{}`$,
$`\delta,I^{\prime})`$

8:    $`\Delta\leftarrow\Delta-\delta`$

9:    if $`\mathsf{P}_{\{\Theta{}\}{}}{}=\bot`$ then

10:     continue

11:    end if

12:    if $`\{\Theta\}\neq\{\}`$ then

13:
    $`({\theta_{1}}^{*},\dots,{\theta_{k}}^{*})\leftarrow{\color[rgb]{0.293,0,0.5117}learn}(\mathsf{P}_{\{\Theta{}\}{}}{},\mathsf{L}{},\mathrm{D})`$

14:
    $`\mathcal{P}\leftarrow\mathcal{P}\cup\{\mathsf{P}_{\{({\theta_{1}}^{*},\dots,{\theta_{k}}^{*})/\Theta\}}{}\}`$

15:    else

16:
    $`\mathcal{P}\leftarrow\mathcal{P}\cup\{\mathsf{P}_{\{\Theta{}\}{}}{}\}`$

17:    end if

18:
   $`I^{\prime}\leftarrow{\color[rgb]{0.293,0,0.5117}collectFeedback}(\mathsf{P}_{\{\Theta{}\}{}}{},\mathrm{D})`$

19: end while

20:
$`{f}^{*}\leftarrow\arg\min_{f\in\mathcal{P}}\sum_{(x,y)\in\mathrm{D}}\mathsf{L}{}(x,y,f(x))`$

21: return $`{f}^{*}`$

Algorithm 2 SEVerA

The resulting tuned agent is added to the candidate pool, and its
execution traces on $`\mathrm{D}`$ are used to construct feedback
$`I^{\prime}`$ (see Appendix
[P](#A16 "Appendix P Planner Feedback ‣ SEVerA: Verified Self-Evolving Agents"))
that guides the planner in subsequent search iterations. After the
search budget $`\Delta`$ is exhausted, SEVerA returns the agent in the
pool that achieves the lowest task loss on the dataset. If
$`\mathcal{P}`$ is empty, SEVerA returns $`\bot`$.

### 5.3. Theoretical Results

The soundness of SEVerA guarantees that any agent program
$`{f}^{*}\neq\bot`$ returned satisfies the behavioral specifications
$`(\Phi,\Psi)`$. The searchVerify step generates candidate programs
$`\mathsf{P}_{\{\Theta{}\}{}}{}`$ that satisfy $`(\Phi,\Psi)`$ for all
$`(\theta_{1},\dots,\theta_{k})\in\{\Theta{}\}{}`$. Consequently, the
parameters $`({\theta_{1}}^{*},\dots,{\theta_{k}}^{*})`$ predicted by
the learning step preserve constraint satisfaction. The pool
$`\mathcal{P}`$ is either empty or contains only programs that satisfy
the behavioral specifications.

###### Theorem 5.4 (Soundness).

If $`{f}^{*}\neq\bot`$ then,
$`\varphi_{\mathcal{A}{}}\implies\forall x_{1}\in T_{1},\dots,\forall x_{n}\in T_{n}.\Phi(x_{1},\dots,x_{n})\implies\Psi(x_{1},\dots,x_{n},{f}^{*}(x_{1},\dots,x_{n}))`$.

###### Proof Sketch.

$`({f}^{*}\neq\bot)\implies({f}^{*}\in\mathcal{P})`$ and all program
$`f\in\mathcal{P}`$ satisfies
$`\varphi_{\mathcal{A}{}}\implies\forall x_{1}\in T_{1},\dots,\forall x_{n}\in T_{n}.\Phi(x_{1},\dots,x_{n})\implies\Psi(x_{1},\dots,x_{n},f(x_{1},\dots,x_{n}))`$
following
Theorem [5.3](#S5.Thmtheorem3 "Theorem 5.3. ‣ 5.2.4. Search and Verify ‣ 5.2. Key Steps ‣ 5. Technical Details ‣ SEVerA: Verified Self-Evolving Agents").
We provide the formal details in
Appendix [R](#A18 "Appendix R Proof Details ‣ SEVerA: Verified Self-Evolving Agents").
∎

Next, we characterize a sufficient condition that ensures the existence
of a candidate solution $`f\in\mathsf{S}(G,\mathcal{F})`$ that satisfies
$`(\Phi,\Psi)`$ and achieves no worse loss $`\mathsf{L}{}`$ than any
generative model $`f_{n}^{\theta}\in\mathcal{F}_{p}`$ with any prompting
function $`f_{p}\in\mathsf{S}(G,\mathcal{F}_{c})`$ and initial
parameters $`\theta_{0}`$. The high-level idea is as follows. If there
exists a non-parametric program
$`f_{d}\in\mathsf{S}(G,\mathcal{F}_{c})`$ that satisfies
$`(\Phi,\Psi)`$, we can use it as a fallback together with any
type-correct generative model $`f_{n}^{\theta}`$ (i.e., with output type
$`T_{o}`$) to construct an FGGM. A program that invokes this FGGM on the
input and returns its output satisfies $`(\Phi,\Psi)`$. Moreover, if
$`{\color[rgb]{0.293,0,0.5117}check_{\mathcal{A},\Phi,\Psi}}{}`$ is
complete and does not incorrectly reject valid samples from
$`f_{n}^{\theta}`$, then the FGGM always returns valid samples from
$`f_{n}^{\theta}`$.
Lemma [5.1](#S5.Thmtheorem1 "Lemma 5.1 (Completeness of Checker). ‣ 5.2.2. FGGM Well-formedness ‣ 5.2. Key Steps ‣ 5. Technical Details ‣ SEVerA: Verified Self-Evolving Agents")
shows that
$`{\color[rgb]{0.293,0,0.5117}check_{\mathcal{A},\Phi,\Psi}}{}`$ is
complete when $`\Psi`$ is quantifier-free. Assume: (i) $`\mathsf{L}{}`$
penalizes constraint-violating outputs more than constraint-satisfying
ones, i.e.,
$`\forall x\in T_{i},\;\forall y,y^{\prime}\in T_{o}.\;(\Phi(x)\wedge\neg\Psi(x,y)\wedge\Psi(x,y^{\prime}))\implies\mathsf{L}{}(x,\_,y^{\prime})<\mathsf{L}{}(x,\_,y)`$,
(ii) $`\Psi`$ is quantifier-free, and (iii) there exists a valid
non-parametric program $`f_{d}`$ satisfying $`(\Phi,\Psi)`$. Then there
exists a program $`f\in\mathsf{S}(G,\mathcal{F})`$ that satisfies
$`(\Phi,\Psi)`$ and incurs no greater loss than any type-correct
generative model $`f_{n}^{\theta}:T_{i}\to T_{o}`$ with initial
parameters. Moreover, if $`f_{n}^{\theta}(x)`$ violates
$`\Psi(x,f_{n}^{\theta}(x))`$ for some $`(x,\_)\in\mathrm{D}`$, the
improvement in loss is strict.

###### Theorem 5.5 (Sufficient Success Condition).

If (i) $`\mathsf{L}{}`$ penalizes constraint violations,
i.e.,$`\forall x\in T_{i},\;\forall y,y^{\prime}\in T_{o}.\;(\Phi(x)\wedge\neg\Psi(x,y)\wedge\Psi(x,y^{\prime}))\implies\mathsf{L}{}(x,\_,y^{\prime})<\mathsf{L}{}(x,\_,y),`$,
(ii) $`\Psi`$ is quantifier-free, (iii) there exists a non-parametric
program $`f_{d}\in\mathsf{S}(G,\mathcal{F}_{c})`$ such that $`f_{d}`$
satisfies $`(\Phi,\Psi)`$. Then, for any type-correct generative model
$`f_{n}^{\theta}:T_{i}\to T_{o}`$ with initial parameters and any
prompting program $`f_{p}{}`$, there exists a program
$`f\in\mathsf{S}(G,\mathcal{F})`$ such that: (1) $`f`$ satisfies
$`(\Phi,\Psi)`$, and (2)
$`\mathsf{L}{}(f)\leq\mathsf{L}{}(f_{n}^{\theta})`$. Moreover, if there
exists $`(x,\_)\in\mathrm{D}`$ such that
$`\neg\Psi(x,f_{n}^{\theta}(x))`$, then
$`\mathsf{L}{}(f)<\mathsf{L}{}(f_{n}^{\theta})`$ where
$`L(f)=\sum_{(x,\_)\in\mathrm{D}}\mathsf{L}{}(x,\_,f(x))`$.

###### Proof Sketch.

Define
$`\mathsf{G}{}=({\color[rgb]{0.293,0,0.5117}id},f_{n}^{\theta},\tau,\Phi_{l},\Psi_{l},f_{p},f_{d},info)`$
where $`(\Phi_{l},\Psi_{l}):=(\Phi,\Psi)`$. Since $`f_{d}`$ satisfies
$`(\Phi,\Psi)`$, the FGGM is valid. Define the program:

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle{\color[rgb]{0,0.3594,0.668}\textbf{function}}\ {\color[rgb]{0.293,0,0.5117}f}(x_{1}:T_{1},\dots,x_{n}:T_{n}):T_{o}\{{\color[rgb]{0,0.3594,0.668}\textbf{return}}\ {\color[rgb]{0.293,0,0.5117}id}(x_{1},\dots,x_{n});\}`$ |  |

For any input satisfying $`\Phi`$, by completeness of
$`{\color[rgb]{0.293,0,0.5117}check_{\mathcal{A},\Phi_{l},\Psi_{l}}}`$
(Lemma [5.1](#S5.Thmtheorem1 "Lemma 5.1 (Completeness of Checker). ‣ 5.2.2. FGGM Well-formedness ‣ 5.2. Key Steps ‣ 5. Technical Details ‣ SEVerA: Verified Self-Evolving Agents")),
$`{\color[rgb]{0.293,0,0.5117}id}`$ returns $`f_{n}^{\theta}(x)`$
whenever $`\Psi(x,f_{n}^{\theta}(x))`$ holds, and otherwise returns
$`f_{d}(x)`$, which satisfies $`\Psi`$. For each
$`(x,\_)\in\mathrm{D}`$, $`f(x)`$ either equals $`f_{n}^{\theta}(x)`$
(if valid) or $`f_{d}(x)`$. By assumption (i), such replacement cannot
increase loss, so $`\mathsf{L}{}(f)\leq\mathsf{L}{}(f_{n}^{\theta})`$.
If $`f_{n}^{\theta}`$ violates $`\Psi`$ on some $`(x,\_)\in\mathrm{D}`$,
the improvement is strict. Formal details in
Appendix [R](#A18 "Appendix R Proof Details ‣ SEVerA: Verified Self-Evolving Agents").
∎

Theorem [5.5](#S5.Thmtheorem5 "Theorem 5.5 (Sufficient Success Condition). ‣ 5.3. Theoretical Results ‣ 5. Technical Details ‣ SEVerA: Verified Self-Evolving Agents")
provides a constructive argument: the FGGM mechanism can always improve
upon a bare GM call by filtering out constraint-violating outputs and
substituting the fallback. The three assumptions are mild in practice.
Assumption (i) requires only that constraint-satisfying outputs are
preferred over violating ones, which holds for any reasonable loss
function in constrained settings. Assumption (ii), requiring
quantifier-free $`\Psi`$, ensures completeness of the checker
$`{\color[rgb]{0.293,0,0.5117}check_{\mathcal{A},\Phi_{l},\Psi_{l}}}`$
(Lemma [5.1](#S5.Thmtheorem1 "Lemma 5.1 (Completeness of Checker). ‣ 5.2.2. FGGM Well-formedness ‣ 5.2. Key Steps ‣ 5. Technical Details ‣ SEVerA: Verified Self-Evolving Agents"))
so that no valid GM outputs are incorrectly rejected. In our
experiments, the symbolic regression task uses quantifier-free
specifications, while the program verification task uses
library-function predicates (e.g.,
$`{\color[rgb]{0.293,0,0.5117}parse}`$,
$`{\color[rgb]{0.293,0,0.5117}noDiff}`$) that are computable on concrete
inputs, effectively behaving as quantifier-free checks at runtime.
Assumption (iii), the existence of a valid fallback, is a natural
requirement: if no non-parametric program can satisfy the specification,
then the specification may be too strong for the given library. The
theorem does not guarantee that SEVerA will *find* the optimal program,
as the planner LLM may not propose the right candidate within the search
budget. Rather, it establishes that the search space
$`\mathsf{S}(G,\mathcal{F})`$ is rich enough to contain solutions that
dominate unconstrained GM calls.

## 6. Evaluation

We evaluate SEVerA on four tasks spanning scientific discovery, program
verification, mathematical reasoning, and agentic tool use. The
evaluation seeks to answer three main questions: whether formal
constraints improve safety, whether learning remains effective under
those constraints, and how conformance tuning with local constraints
improves performance.

### 6.1. Experimental Setup

#### 6.1.1. Tasks and Datasets

We instantiate SEVerA on four tasks, each representative of a different
kind of constrained agent synthesis problem.

LLM-Assisted Program Verification (DafnyBench). The agent receives a
Dafny program with pre-encoded input-output specifications and must
synthesize annotations that enable verification against the pre-encoded
specification inside the input program ([Loughridge et al.,
2025](#bib.bib36)). The behavioral specification of the agent requires
the output to remain parsable and equivalent to the input modulo added
annotations. The task performance is measured by verification success
within a fixed time budget. The underlying LLM is Claude Sonnet 4.5
([Anthropic, 2025](#bib.bib52)), a closed-source model whose weights are
not accessible; consequently, the learning step (i.e., parameter tuning)
is not applicable to this task.

Symbolic Math Synthesis (GSM-Symbolic). GSM-Symbolic is a benchmark of
grade-school math word problems generated from symbolic templates
([Mirzadeh et al., 2024](#bib.bib50)). We use it to evaluate the LLM’s
ability to synthesize correct symbolic mathematical expressions.
Behavioral specification of the agent enforces that each generated
expression is syntactically valid with respect to a formal grammar, and
task performance measures whether the answer is equivalent to the
ground-truth expression.

Agentic Tool Use ($`\tau^{2}`$-bench). $`\tau^{2}`$-bench ([Barres et
al., 2025](#bib.bib49)) evaluates conversational LLM agents in realistic
customer-service scenarios. We use the retail and airlines domains. The
agent must select and invoke API tools to resolve user requests while
respecting domain-specific policies. Unlike the other tasks, the hard
constraint and the utility metric operate at different granularities.
The hard constraint is enforced at each individual tool call: before
every tool call is executed, the Agent-C checker ([Kamath et al.,
2025](#bib.bib29)) verifies that the proposed call complies with
temporal policy-compliance rules (e.g., refund eligibility,
booking-modification policies) given the trace of prior calls. Task
performance (pass rate) is measured over the entire multi-turn
interaction trace as the percentage of interactions where the agent
successfully resolves the user request.

Constrained Symbolic Regression (SymReg). In symbolic regression, each
synthesis instance consists of noisy input–output observations generated
by an unknown ground-truth function $`f_{gt}`$, along with a behavioral
specification encoding prior knowledge about $`f_{gt}`$. The goal is to
synthesize a neuro-symbolic program (i.e., the agent) that fits the
observed input–output pairs while provably satisfying the behavioral
specifications. We consider a total of $`35`$ synthesis tasks, each with
$`2`$ different training sets corresponding to varying noise levels
$`(5\%,10\%)`$, and behavioral specifications that encode symbolic
bounds on the ground truth. Each training set includes $`600`$ noisy
samples and $`400`$ test samples. All synthesis instances are drawn from
popular benchmarks ([Haider and Kronberger, 2022](#bib.bib41); [Błądek
and Krawiec, 2019](#bib.bib34)).

#### 6.1.2. Implementation Details

All experiments are conducted on NVIDIA A100 GPUs (40 GB). Across all
tasks we use the same high-level pipeline: planner-guided program search
with a budget of $`\Delta=10`$ iterations, FGGM-based rejection sampling
with a fixed sample budget $`K=5`$, deductive verification with bounded
verifier and SMT timeouts, and hyperparameter tuning when model
parameters are accessible. The planner LLM is provided with 3
ground-truth examples as in-context examples (2 for $`\tau^{2}`$-bench,
due to the long traces); these examples are excluded from all train and
test splits. The full planner prompt template is given in
Appendix [Q](#A17 "Appendix Q Planner LLM Prompt ‣ SEVerA: Verified Self-Evolving Agents"),
and details on how execution feedback is constructed and provided to the
planner between iterations are given in
Appendix [P](#A16 "Appendix P Planner Feedback ‣ SEVerA: Verified Self-Evolving Agents").

#### 6.1.3. Learning Implementation

Once a program verifies, SEVerA uses Dafny’s built-in transpiler ([Dafny
Language Community, 2023](#bib.bib17)) to translate the verified code
into Python. Parameter tuning and experiments are then conducted on the
transpiled code. SEVerA assumes that Dafny’s transpiler is sound for
this restricted subset of the language.

#### 6.1.4. Metrics

For each task, we report: (a) the constraint violation rate on a
held-out test set of unseen inputs, measuring the fraction of outputs
that violate the behavioral specification $`(\Phi,\Psi)`$; (b) task
performance, measured by mean squared error for SymReg, verification
success rate for Dafny, answer accuracy for GSM-Symbolic, and pass rate
for $`\tau^{2}`$-Bench; and (c) wall-clock time.

#### 6.1.5. Baseline

For all four tasks outside GSM-symbolic, we consider state-of-the-art
(SOTA) hand-crafted agents. For GSM-Symbolic, we use the SOTA
constrained decoder ([Banerjee et al., 2025](#bib.bib45)). Some
hand-crafted agents (e.g., Agent-C on $`\tau^{2}`$-Bench) manually
enforce hard constraints; however, being static, they achieve lower task
performance. We also consider self-evolving frameworks without
constraints, which do not verify the generated programs against
behavioral specifications and accept all planner programs provided they
are syntactically valid and type-checked. Consequently, such frameworks
provide no guarantees about the correctness or safety of the generated
code. To ensure fairness, unconstrained self-evolving frameworks are
only allowed to use the same set of library functions.

#### 6.1.6. Verification Success

For program verification, tool calling, and GSM-Symbolic, SEVerA
consistently finds a valid program satisfying $`(\Phi,\Psi)`$ within
$`10`$ attempts. For symbolic regression, it produces a verified program
in $`33`$ out of $`35`$ cases, whereas the baselines generate at least
$`11`$ cases where the generated program violates the behavioral
specification on test inputs.

| Dataset                    | Total | Train |
|----------------------------|-------|-------|
| HumanEvalDafny             | 135   | 30    |
| DafnyBench                 | 760   | 50    |
| $`\tau^{2}`$-bench Retail  | 114   | 15    |
| $`\tau^{2}`$-bench Airline | 50    | 10    |
| GSM-Symbolic               | 100   | 50    |
| Symbolic Regression        | 600   | 400   |

Table 1. Dataset sizes and train/test splits.

#### 6.1.7. Dataset splits.

Table [1](#S6.T1 "Table 1 ‣ 6.1.6. Verification Success ‣ 6.1. Experimental Setup ‣ 6. Evaluation ‣ SEVerA: Verified Self-Evolving Agents")
summarizes the dataset sizes for each synthesis task. For each task, a
small training set is used for the learning step and the remaining
examples form the held-out test set on which all reported metrics are
computed. GSM-Symbolic uses a larger training fraction (50%) because its
learning step performs GRPO-based fine-tuning, which requires more
training data than the other tasks.

#### 6.1.8. Task-specific details.

For Dafny, the underlying LLM is Claude Sonnet 4.5 ([Anthropic,
2025](#bib.bib52)), a closed-source model; because model weights are
inaccessible, Dafny experiments use only the search and verification
stages of SEVerA and do not perform parameter tuning. For
$`\tau^{2}`$-bench, parameter tuning is also omitted because the long,
multi-turn execution traces make gradient-based fine-tuning
prohibitively expensive. For GSM-Symbolic, the learning step uses GRPO
([Shao et al., 2024](#bib.bib22)) with LoRA adapters ([Hu et al.,
2022](#bib.bib51)) on Qwen3-8B ([Team, 2025](#bib.bib53)). Additional
hyperparameters (LoRA rank, solver timeouts, etc.) are reported in
Appendix [O](#A15 "Appendix O Hyperparameters ‣ SEVerA: Verified Self-Evolving Agents").

### 6.2. Main Results

We begin with the central question motivating SEVerA:

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

We compare unconstrained agent synthesis against SEVerA across all four
tasks to show that hard behavioral specifications are necessary: without
them, agents silently produce invalid outputs on unseen inputs that are
undetectable by soft performance metrics.

Table 2. Dafny program verification results on HumanEvalDafny and
DafnyBench. *Verif. & NoDiff* counts a program as correct only if it
both verifies and passes the AST-based diff check against the original;
*Verif.* counts verification alone.

Table [2](#S6.T2 "Table 2 ‣ 6.2.1. LLM-Assisted Program Verification (Dafny) ‣ 6.2. Main Results ‣ 6. Evaluation ‣ SEVerA: Verified Self-Evolving Agents")
presents results on two Dafny program-verification benchmarks and offers
the clearest illustration of why formal constraints are indispensable.
The gap between the *Verif.* and *Verif. & NoDiff* columns reveals the
core safety issue (RQ1): without hard constraints, agents inflate their
verification rate by modifying the original program. The LLM baseline
reports 76.8% verification on HumanEvalDafny, yet only 73.7% of those
outputs actually preserve the input program. Overall, 8.1% of all
outputs are violations that would go undetected by a metric that checks
verification alone. The DafnyBench baseline and SEVerA without
constraints reduce but do not eliminate this problem (4.0% and 5.1%
violations, respectively). Only the full SEVerA pipeline, which enforces
the *NoDiff* behavioral specification, achieves a 0% violation rate on
both benchmarks while simultaneously attaining the highest Verif. &
NoDiff rate (97.0% on HumanEvalDafny, 89.1% on DafnyBench). This
confirms that FGGM-based rejection sampling with a verified fallback
does not merely filter outputs but actively steers the planner toward
higher-quality candidates. This result is particularly notable because
it is achieved without any parameter tuning (the underlying model,
Claude Sonnet 4.5, is closed-source), the gains come entirely from
making constraints visible to the planner and enforcing them at
synthesis time. The overhead introduced by SEVerA is modest. The full
pipeline takes 18.2 s per instance on HumanEvalDafny compared to 9.8 s
for LLM generation, roughly a $`1.9\times`$ factor that includes Dafny
verification and up to $`k`$ LLM calls. On DafnyBench the factor is
$`2.5\times`$ (25.6 s vs. 10.3 s). Given that the LLM baseline produces
untrustworthy outputs on 8 to 10% of inputs, we believe this overhead is
justified for the formal guarantees it provides.
