````math
Table 3. $`\tau^{2}`$-bench results with Qwen3-8B on the retail and
airline domains. Higher pass rate is better; lower violation rate is
better.

Table [3](#S6.T3 "Table 3 ‣ 6.2.2. Agentic Tool Use (𝜏^2-bench) ‣ 6.2. Main Results ‣ 6. Evaluation ‣ SEVerA: Verified Self-Evolving Agents")
reports performance on $`\tau^{2}`$-bench. The LLM baseline (Qwen3-8B
without constraints) violates domain policies on 76.3% of retail
interactions and 68.4% of airline interactions, yielding pass rates of
only 11.3% and 13.2%, respectively. Both Agent-C and SEVerA reduce the
violation rate to 0%, confirming that formal policy enforcement is
necessary. SEVerA without constraints illustrates an intermediate point:
by running the search loop without informing the planner of the policy
specification, SEVerA (w/o constraints) improves pass rates to 49.4%
(retail) and 44.7% (airline), but still incurs 10.3% and 25.5% violation
rates, respectively. Enforcing constraints eliminates all violations
while further improving pass rates to 53.6% and 52.6%. This gap reflects
SEVerA’s search-verify-learn design. By synthesizing agent programs that
are verified to satisfy the per-call policy specification, SEVerA can
explore a wider space of compliant strategies rather than relying solely
on runtime constraint checking. The per-call hard constraint ensures
that every individual tool call is policy-compliant, while the search
loop optimizes the agent’s overall strategy to maximize the end-of-trace
pass rate. Impressively, SEVerA with the small open-weight Qwen3-8B
outperforms Agent-C ([Kamath et al., 2025](#bib.bib29)) with Claude
Sonnet 4.5 (52.6 vs 47.3).

SEVerA is also faster than Agent-C in both domains (212.4s vs. 234.7s in
retail and 241.1s vs. 272.6s in airline). The LLM baseline is fastest
because it performs no policy checking, but its outputs are unusable in
practice given the violation rates.

#### 6.2.3. Symbolic Math Synthesis (GSM-Symbolic)

GSM-Symbolic uses Qwen3-8B as the underlying LLM. Qwen3-8B is
open-weight, making parameter tuning feasible. This allows us to ask:

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

| Method | Accuracy (%) $`\uparrow`$ |  | Violation (%) $`\downarrow`$ |  | Time (s) |
|----|----|----|----|----|----|
| LLM (Qwen3-8B) | 38.3 |  | 10.6 |  | 10.9 |
| CRANE ([Banerjee et al., 2025](#bib.bib45)) | 44.7 |  | 2.1 |  | 12.4 |
| SEVerA (no parameter tuning) | 53.2 | (+8.5) | 0.0 | (-2.1) | 18.8 |
| SEVerA (with parameter tuning) | 66.0 | (+21.3) | 0.0 | (-2.1) | 16.7 |

Table 4. GSM-Symbolic results with Qwen3-8B. Higher accuracy is better;
lower violation rate is better.

Table [4](#S6.T4 "Table 4 ‣ 6.2.3. Symbolic Math Synthesis (GSM-Symbolic) ‣ 6.2. Main Results ‣ 6. Evaluation ‣ SEVerA: Verified Self-Evolving Agents")
compares SEVerA against the LLM baseline and CRANE ([Banerjee et al.,
2025](#bib.bib45)), a state-of-the-art constrained-decoding method, on
GSM-Symbolic using Qwen3-8B. The LLM baseline (Qwen3-8B) achieves only
38.3% accuracy with a 10.6% constraint violation rate (RQ1), confirming
that a vanilla LLM frequently produces outputs that are syntactically or
semantically invalid. CRANE improves accuracy to 44.7% and reduces
violations to 2.1% by augmenting the output grammar with reasoning
tokens. ¹¹ 1 CRANE only ensures that at every decoding step, the
generated partial output is a valid prefix of the target grammar.SEVerA
without parameter tuning already achieves 53.2% accuracy and eliminates
all violations, an 8.5% accuracy improvement over CRANE with strictly
stronger correctness guarantees. This improvement stems from the FGGM
mechanism: the rejection sampler with a verified fallback ensures that
every output satisfies the formal grammar and the semantic
specification, while the synthesized prompting program $`f_{p}`$ guides
the underlying LLM toward correct answers.

We also compare the performance of SEVerA with and without parameter
tuning (RQ2). We fine-tune Qwen3-8B via GRPO with LoRA adapters under
the same formal constraints. This provides a further 12.8% accuracy gain
(from 53.2% to 66.0%) while maintaining the zero-violation guarantee.
The tuned model produces outputs that more often pass the FGGM checker
$`{\color[rgb]{0.293,0,0.5117}check_{\mathcal{A},\Phi_{l},\Psi_{l}}}`$
on the first sample, reducing reliance on the fallback and thereby
improving answer quality. Notably, the tuned variant is also faster than
the untuned one (16.7 s vs. 18.8 s), because higher conformance reduces
the number of rejection-sampling iterations needed per call.

#### 6.2.4. Constrained Symbolic Regression

In constrained symbolic regression, we consider the SOTA genetic
programming–based method PySR ([Cranmer, 2023](#bib.bib15)), as well as
the existing self-evolving method LLM-SR ([Shojaee et al.,
2025](#bib.bib16)), which samples parametric programs with optimizable
PyTorch parameters and refines them to minimize loss. We denote the
noise level by $`\epsilon`$. As shown in
Table [6](#S6.T6 "Table 6 ‣ 6.2.4. Constrained Symbolic Regression ‣ 6.2. Main Results ‣ 6. Evaluation ‣ SEVerA: Verified Self-Evolving Agents"),
both baselines frequently produce programs that violate the behavioral
specifications on the test data, with violations occurring in up to
$`62.86\%`$ of synthesis instances for PySR and up to $`34.29\%`$ for
LLM-SR. For both noise levels, SEVerA finds a verified solution in
$`33`$ out of $`35`$ instances.
Table [6](#S6.T6 "Table 6 ‣ 6.2.4. Constrained Symbolic Regression ‣ 6.2. Main Results ‣ 6. Evaluation ‣ SEVerA: Verified Self-Evolving Agents")
presents a pairwise comparison between SEVerA and the baselines in terms
of normalized mean squared error (NMSE) on the test dataset. We compute
the average NMSE over only those instances where the baseline-generated
programs satisfy the behavioral constraints, pruning instances that
correspond to invalid solutions. SEVerA achieves significantly lower
NMSE values compared to both baselines.

| Method | $`\epsilon`$ (5%) $`\downarrow`$ | $`\epsilon`$ (10%) $`\downarrow`$ |
|--------|----------------------------------|-----------------------------------|
| PySR   | 62.86%                           | 62.86%                            |
| LLM-SR | 31.43%                           | 34.29%                            |
| SEVerA | 0.00%                            | 0.00%                             |

Table 5. % of synthesised instances that violate behavioral
specifications on the test set.

| Comparison | $`\epsilon=0.05`$ |          | $`\epsilon=0.1`$ |          |
|------------|-------------------|----------|------------------|----------|
|            | SEVerA            | Baseline | SEVerA           | Baseline |
| vs PySR    | 0.0593            | 0.3113   | 0.0879           | 0.1217   |
| vs LLM-SR  | 0.0200            | 0.1580   | 0.0205           | 0.1583   |

Table 6. NMSE values averaged over all instances that do not violate
constraints on test data.

### 6.3. Constraint Decomposition

The previous section showed that formal constraints improve both safety
and performance. We now ask a finer-grained question:

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

| Configuration | Accuracy (%) $`\uparrow`$ |  | Violation (%) $`\downarrow`$ |  |
|----|----|----|----|----|
| LLM (Qwen3-8B) | 38.3 |  | 10.6 |  |
| SEVerA (no parameter tuning) | 53.2 | (+14.9) | 0.0 | (-10.6) |
| SEVerA (local only parameter tuning) | 55.3 | (+17.0) | 0.0 | (-10.6) |
| SEVerA (global only parameter tuning) | 61.7 | (+23.4) | 0.0 | (-10.6) |
| SEVerA (full) | 66.0 | (+27.7) | 0.0 | (-10.6) |

Table 7. Constraint decomposition ablation on GSM-Symbolic (Qwen3-8B).
*Local* = FGGM contracts only; *Global* = behavioral specification only;
*Full* = both.

We ablate each component independently on GSM-Symbolic.
Table [7](#S6.T7 "Table 7 ‣ 6.3. Constraint Decomposition ‣ 6. Evaluation ‣ SEVerA: Verified Self-Evolving Agents")
decomposes the 12.8% gain that parameter tuning provides (from 53.2% to
66.0%, as shown in
Table [4](#S6.T4 "Table 4 ‣ 6.2.3. Symbolic Math Synthesis (GSM-Symbolic) ‣ 6.2. Main Results ‣ 6. Evaluation ‣ SEVerA: Verified Self-Evolving Agents"))
into its two sources. Starting from SEVerA without parameter tuning
(53.2%), adding *local-only* tuning, which optimizes the FGGM
conformance loss so that the model’s outputs more frequently satisfy
per-call contracts, yields a modest improvement to 55.3%. This 2.1% gain
indicates that parameter tuning alone helps the model produce
syntactically valid outputs more reliably, reducing reliance on
rejection sampling. *Global-only* tuning, which optimizes the task loss
$`\mathsf{L}{}`$ without the FGGM conformance component, provides a
substantially larger gain to 61.7%. This 8.5% improvement reflects the
direct benefit of training the model to produce semantically correct
answers. The full SEVerA pipeline combines both losses and achieves
66.0%, a 4.3% gain. This demonstrates that the two training signals are
complementary: global tuning improves answer correctness while local
conformance tuning ensures outputs satisfy per-call contracts, jointly
yielding the best overall accuracy.

### 6.4. Example Synthesized Agent

We provide a complete agent program synthesised by SEVerA for the
DafnyBench task in
Appendix [K](#A11 "Appendix K Example Agents for LLM Assisted Program Verification ‣ SEVerA: Verified Self-Evolving Agents").
The agent defines three FGGMs:
$`{\color[rgb]{0.293,0,0.5117}initialFGGM}`$,
$`{\color[rgb]{0.293,0,0.5117}diffErrorFGGM}`$, and
$`{\color[rgb]{0.293,0,0.5117}verifierErrorFGGM}`$. Each sharing the
local output contract
$`\Psi_{l}:={\color[rgb]{0.293,0,0.5117}noDiff}(base\_program,\cdot)`$
and differing only in their prompting function $`f_{p}`$, which
specialises the LLM prompt for initial annotation, diff-checker repair,
and verifier-error repair, respectively. The resulting agent program is
verified to provably comply with the diff-checker specification for all
inputs and all parameter values, ensuring that no synthesised output
modifies the original program beyond adding annotations.

### 6.5. Discussion

Across all four tasks, SEVerA achieves zero constraint violations on
held-out test inputs while simultaneously improving task performance
over every baseline. These results confirm that formal behavioral
specifications do not merely enforce safety but actively prune the space
of candidate programs, steering synthesis toward higher-quality agents.
SEVerA’s runtime overhead is competitive: on $`\tau^{2}`$-bench it is
*faster* than Agent-C, and on Dafny and GSM-Symbolic the full pipeline
introduces a modest $`1.9`$–$`2.5\times`$ slowdown relative to the LLM
baseline, attributable to the verification and rejection-sampling steps.
One current limitation is that the formulation is *resource-unaware*:
behavioral specifications constrain functional correctness but do not
account for computational resources such as LLM calls, token usage, or
wall-clock budget. Extending SEVerA with resource-bound specifications
([Knoth et al., 2019](#bib.bib40)), for example by encoding token or
call budgets as additional hard constraints within the FGGM framework,
is a promising direction for future work.

## 7. Related Work

Self-Evolving Agents and Their Risks. Recent work has explored automatic
agent synthesis and self-improvement, from code-based action
unification ([Wang et al., 2024](#bib.bib1)) and open-ended skill
libraries ([Wang et al., 2023](#bib.bib2)) to architecture search ([Hu
et al., 2025](#bib.bib3); [Zhuge et al., 2024](#bib.bib5); [Gao et al.,
2025](#bib.bib6)), gradient-free symbolic updates ([Zhou et al.,
2024](#bib.bib7)), co-evolution with world models ([Fang et al.,
2025](#bib.bib8)), and reinforcement-learning-driven skill
refinement ([Wang et al., 2026](#bib.bib9); [Tian et al.,
2025](#bib.bib10)). However, none of these provide formal behavioral
guarantees, a gap made urgent by demonstrated risks of coding-agent
exploits ([Guo et al., 2024](#bib.bib11); [Lee et al.,
2025](#bib.bib12); [Guardian, 2026](#bib.bib13)), test-case
exploitation ([Zhong et al., 2025](#bib.bib48)), and verification
cheating ([Banerjee et al., 2026](#bib.bib44)). SEVerA addresses this by
imposing and verifying hard formal specifications before deployment.

Runtime Monitoring and Shielding. Rather than verifying at synthesis
time, runtime approaches enforce safety on observed executions. Shield
synthesis from neural policies ([Zhu et al., 2019](#bib.bib47)) and
temporal-logic runtime checking of tool-call sequences ([Kamath et al.,
2025](#bib.bib29)) are representative examples, but both are limited to
observed traces and cannot guarantee safety on unseen inputs. SEVerA
instead verifies the synthesized program for *all* inputs and parameter
values at synthesis time. The monitoring checks can be used to define
the specification as done with ([Kamath et al., 2025](#bib.bib29)).

Neuro-Symbolic Program Synthesis. Neuro-symbolic methods, including
neural program generation from examples ([Parisotto et al.,
2016](#bib.bib46)), type-directed differentiable programming ([Valkov et
al., 2018](#bib.bib23)), wake-sleep library learning ([Ellis et al.,
2021](#bib.bib39)), vision-language program composition ([Surís et al.,
2023](#bib.bib4)), and LLM-guided symbolic regression ([Shojaee et al.,
2025](#bib.bib16)), synthesize programs that invoke neural components
but lack formal correctness guarantees over the composed system. SEVerA
extends this paradigm with FGGMs that bind each model call to a verified
local contract, enabling end-to-end verification.

Constrained Decoding. Constrained decoding restricts LLM outputs to a
formal language through grammar-based ([Ugare et al.,
2025b](#bib.bib24); [Park et al., 2024](#bib.bib25); [Ugare et al.,
2025a](#bib.bib27)), diffusion-based ([Suresh et al.,
2025](#bib.bib26)), programming-abstraction ([Beurer-Kellner et al.,
2023](#bib.bib32); [Khattab et al., 2024](#bib.bib33)),
reasoning-preserving ([Banerjee et al., 2025](#bib.bib45)),
type-based ([Mündler et al., 2025](#bib.bib42)), and semantic ([Nagy et
al., 2026](#bib.bib43)) techniques. These approaches require access to
the model’s decoding internals (precluding closed-source models) and
enforce per-token or per-output constraints, not program-level
behavioral specifications. SEVerA’s FGGM mechanism operates on model
outputs via rejection sampling, supports rich first-order logic
specifications verified at the program level, and is model-agnostic.

Deductive Program Synthesis. Classical deductive synthesis, including
syntax-guided ([Alur et al., 2013](#bib.bib14)), semantics-guided ([Kim
et al., 2021](#bib.bib18)), counterexample-guided ([Solar-Lezama,
2013](#bib.bib20)), abstraction-guided ([Guria et al.,
2023](#bib.bib19)), and component-based ([Feng et al.,
2017](#bib.bib21)) approaches, provides strong correctness guarantees
but targets deterministic, non-parametric programs. SEVerA bridges this
gap with a CEGIS-style search–verify loop for program structure while
using FGGMs to encapsulate parametric generative models within verified
contracts.

## 8. Conclusion

We presented SEVerA, a framework for synthesizing self-evolving LLM
agents with formal behavioral guarantees. By introducing Formally
Guarded Generative Models (FGGMs), SEVerA binds each generative model
call to a verified local contract backed by a rejection sampler with a
provably correct fallback, ensuring that specifications hold for all
inputs and all parameter values. This design decomposes the constrained
learning problem into a CEGIS-style discrete search over program
structure followed by unconstrained gradient-based parameter
optimization, retaining the scalability of modern fine-tuning methods
such as GRPO while providing end-to-end correctness guarantees. Our
evaluation across constrained symbolic regression, LLM-assisted Dafny
verification, symbolic math synthesis, and policy-compliant agentic tool
use demonstrates that SEVerA achieves zero constraint violations on all
tasks while simultaneously improving task performance over unconstrained
and state-of-the-art baselines. These results show that formal
behavioral constraints are not merely a safety mechanism but an active
guide that prunes the search space and steers synthesis toward
higher-quality agents.

## Appendix A Restricted Dafny Grammar

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\begin{array}[]{rcl}\langle program\rangle&::=&\langle method\_decl\rangle\mid\langle function\_decl\rangle\\[3.44444pt]
\langle method\_decl\rangle&::=&{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\texttt{method}}\ \langle ident\rangle\texttt{(}\langle params\rangle\texttt{)}\ \langle specs\rangle\ \texttt{\lx@text@lbrace}\langle stmt\_list\rangle\texttt{\lx@text@rbrace}\\[3.44444pt]
\langle function\_decl\rangle&::=&{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\texttt{function}}\ \langle ident\rangle\texttt{(}\langle params\rangle\texttt{)}:\langle type\rangle\ \langle specs\rangle\ \langle expr\rangle\\[3.44444pt]
\langle params\rangle&::=&\epsilon\mid\langle param\rangle\mid\langle param\rangle,\langle params\rangle\\[3.44444pt]
\langle param\rangle&::=&\langle ident\rangle:\langle type\rangle\\[3.44444pt]
\langle type\rangle&::=&{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\texttt{int}}\mid{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\texttt{bool}}\mid{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\texttt{string}}\mid{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\texttt{real}}\\[3.44444pt]
\langle specs\rangle&::=&\epsilon\mid\langle spec\rangle\langle specs\rangle\\[3.44444pt]
\langle spec\rangle&::=&{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\texttt{requires}}\ \langle formula\rangle\mid{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\texttt{ensures}}\ \langle formula\rangle\\[3.44444pt]
\langle stmt\_list\rangle&::=&\epsilon\mid\langle stmt\rangle\langle stmt\_list\rangle\\[3.44444pt]
\langle stmt\rangle&::=&\langle assign\_stmt\rangle\mid\langle if\_stmt\rangle\mid\langle while\_stmt\rangle\mid\langle assert\_stmt\rangle\mid\langle call\_stmt\rangle\\[3.44444pt]
\langle assign\_stmt\rangle&::=&\langle ident\rangle:=\langle expr\rangle;\\[3.44444pt]
\langle call\_stmt\rangle&::=&\langle ident\rangle\texttt{(}\langle args\rangle\texttt{)};\\[3.44444pt]
\langle args\rangle&::=&\epsilon\mid\langle expr\rangle\mid\langle expr\rangle,\langle args\rangle\\[3.44444pt]
\langle if\_stmt\rangle&::=&{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\texttt{if}}\ \texttt{(}\langle formula\rangle\texttt{)}\texttt{\lx@text@lbrace}\langle stmt\_list\rangle\texttt{\lx@text@rbrace}\\
&&\mid{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\texttt{if}}\ \texttt{(}\langle formula\rangle\texttt{)}\texttt{\lx@text@lbrace}\langle stmt\_list\rangle\texttt{\lx@text@rbrace}\ {\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\texttt{else}}\ \texttt{\lx@text@lbrace}\langle stmt\_list\rangle\texttt{\lx@text@rbrace}\\[3.44444pt]
\langle while\_stmt\rangle&::=&{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\texttt{while}}\ \texttt{(}\langle formula\rangle\texttt{)}\ \langle loop\_annots\rangle\ \texttt{\lx@text@lbrace}\langle stmt\_list\rangle\texttt{\lx@text@rbrace}\\[3.44444pt]
\langle loop\_annots\rangle&::=&\epsilon\mid\langle loop\_annot\rangle\langle loop\_annots\rangle\\[3.44444pt]
\langle loop\_annot\rangle&::=&{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\texttt{invariant}}\ \langle formula\rangle\mid{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\texttt{decreases}}\ \langle expr\rangle\\[3.44444pt]
\langle assert\_stmt\rangle&::=&{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\texttt{assert}}\ \langle formula\rangle;\\[3.44444pt]
\langle expr\rangle&::=&\langle aexpr\rangle\mid\langle sexpr\rangle\\[3.44444pt]
\langle aexpr\rangle&::=&\langle int\_lit\rangle\mid\langle ident\rangle\mid\langle aexpr\rangle\;\langle arith\_op\rangle\;\langle aexpr\rangle\mid(\langle aexpr\rangle)\mid\langle ident\rangle(\langle args\rangle)\\[3.44444pt]
\langle sexpr\rangle&::=&\langle string\_lit\rangle\mid\langle ident\rangle\mid(\langle sexpr\rangle)\mid\langle ident\rangle(\langle args\rangle)\\[3.44444pt]
\langle formula\rangle&::=&\langle expr\rangle\;\langle rel\_op\rangle\;\langle expr\rangle\\
&|&!\;\langle formula\rangle\\
&|&(\langle formula\rangle)\\
&|&\langle ident\rangle(\langle args\rangle)\\
&|&{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\texttt{forall}}\;\langle bound\_vars\rangle::\langle formula\rangle\\
&|&{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\texttt{exists}}\;\langle bound\_vars\rangle::\langle formula\rangle\\[3.44444pt]
\langle bound\_vars\rangle&::=&\langle ident\rangle:\langle type\rangle\mid\langle ident\rangle:\langle type\rangle,\langle bound\_vars\rangle\\[3.44444pt]
\langle arith\_op\rangle&::=&+\mid-\mid*\mid/\\[3.44444pt]
\langle rel\_op\rangle&::=&=\mid\neq\mid<\mid>\mid\leq\mid\geq\\[3.44444pt]
\langle literal\rangle&::=&\langle int\_lit\rangle\mid\langle string\_lit\rangle\mid{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\texttt{true}}\mid{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\texttt{false}}\\[3.44444pt]
\langle int\_lit\rangle&::=&\texttt{0}\mid\texttt{1}\mid\cdots\mid\texttt{9}\text{ (and sequences thereof)}\\[3.44444pt]
\langle string\_lit\rangle&::=&"\langle char\rangle^{*}"\\[3.44444pt]
\langle ident\rangle&::=&\langle letter\rangle\mid\langle letter\rangle\langle ident\rangle\\[3.44444pt]
\langle letter\rangle&::=&a\mid b\mid\cdots\mid z\mid A\mid B\mid\cdots\mid Z\\[3.44444pt]
\langle digit\rangle&::=&0\mid 1\mid\cdots\mid 9\end{array}
``` |  |

## Appendix B Rejection Sampling Details

##### Rejection Sampling Details.

Given a target distribution $`\pi_{t}`$ and a proposal distribution
$`\pi_{p}`$ with $`S(\pi_{t})\subseteq S(\pi_{p})`$, assume there exists
$`M\geq 1`$ such that
$`\forall z\in\Omega,\quad D_{\pi_{t}}(z)\leq M\cdot D_{\pi_{p}}(z).`$
The procedure samples $`z\sim\pi_{p}`$ and
$`u\sim\mathrm{Uniform}(0,1)`$, and accepts $`z`$ iff
$`u\leq\frac{D_{\pi_{t}}(z)}{M\cdot D_{\pi_{p}}(z)}.`$ Otherwise, the
sample is rejected and the process repeats. Accepted samples follow
$`\pi_{t}`$. Moreover, any $`z\notin S(\pi_{t})`$ is always rejected
since $`D_{\pi_{t}}(z)=0`$, ensuring all accepted samples lie in
$`S(\pi_{t})`$. The acceptance probability is $`1/M`$, so efficiency
depends on how tightly $`\pi_{p}`$ upper-bounds $`\pi_{t}`$. For this
paper, we assume $`M=1`$.

- •

  ensures $`r\geq 0`$ ensures $`r=x\lor r=-x`$

  ensures $`(x\leq r)\land(y\leq r)`$ ensures $`(r=x)\lor(r=y)`$

  $`{\color[rgb]{0.293,0,0.5117}min}(x:{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}real},y:{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}real})\rightarrow r:{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}real}`$
  ensures $`(x\geq r)\land(y\geq r)`$ ensures $`(r=x)\lor(r=y)`$
- •
  $`{\color[rgb]{0.293,0,0.5117}sin}(x:{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}real})\rightarrow r:{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}real}`$
  ensures $`-1\leq r\leq 1`$ ensures $`(x=0)\Rightarrow(r=0)`$
- •
  $`{\color[rgb]{0.293,0,0.5117}cos}(x:{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}real})\rightarrow r:{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}real}`$
  ensures $`-1\leq r\leq 1`$ ensures $`(x=0)\Rightarrow(r=1)`$
- •
  $`{\color[rgb]{0.293,0,0.5117}pi}(x:{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}real})\rightarrow r:{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}real}`$
  requires $`x\geq 0`$ ensures $`3.141592653589790\cdot x\leq r`$
  ensures $`r\leq 3.141592653589793\cdot x`$
- •
  $`{\color[rgb]{0.293,0,0.5117}pow}(x:{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}real},d:{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}real})\rightarrow r:{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}real}`$
  requires $`x\geq 0`$ requires $`(x\neq 0)\lor(d\geq 0)`$ ensures
  $`r\geq 0`$ ensures $`(x>0)\Rightarrow(r>0)`$ ensures
  $`(d=0)\Rightarrow(r=1)`$ ensures
  $`(x\geq 1\land d\geq 0)\Rightarrow(r\geq 1)`$ ensures
  $`(x\geq 1\land d\leq 0)\Rightarrow(r\leq 1)`$ ensures
  $`(x\leq 1\land d\geq 0)\Rightarrow(r\leq 1)`$ ensures
  $`(x\leq 1\land d\leq 0)\Rightarrow(r\geq 1)`$

  $`{\color[rgb]{0.293,0,0.5117}sqrt}(x:{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}real})\rightarrow r:{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}real}`$

  ensures $`r\geq 0`$ ensures $`(x\leq 0)\Rightarrow(r\leq 1)`$ ensures
  $`(x\geq 0)\Rightarrow(r\geq 1)`$ ensures
  $`(x=1)\Rightarrow(2.71\leq r\leq 2.72)`$ ensures $`r\geq(1+x)`$
- •
  $`{\color[rgb]{0.293,0,0.5117}log}(x:{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}real})\rightarrow r:{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}real}`$
  requires $`x>0`$ ensures $`(x\geq 1)\Rightarrow(r\geq 0)`$ ensures
  $`(x\leq 1)\Rightarrow(r\leq 0)`$ ensures $`(x=1)\Rightarrow(r=0)`$

## Appendix K Example Agents for LLM Assisted Program Verification

The following is an example verified agent program for the Dafny program
verification task. The agent defines and invokes three
FGGMs—$`{\color[rgb]{0.293,0,0.5117}initialFGGM}`$
(Fig. [4](#A11.F4 "Figure 4 ‣ Appendix K Example Agents for LLM Assisted Program Verification ‣ SEVerA: Verified Self-Evolving Agents")),
$`{\color[rgb]{0.293,0,0.5117}diffErrorFGGM}`$
(Fig. [5](#A11.F5 "Figure 5 ‣ Appendix K Example Agents for LLM Assisted Program Verification ‣ SEVerA: Verified Self-Evolving Agents")),
and $`{\color[rgb]{0.293,0,0.5117}verifierErrorFGGM}`$
(Fig. [6](#A11.F6 "Figure 6 ‣ Appendix K Example Agents for LLM Assisted Program Verification ‣ SEVerA: Verified Self-Evolving Agents"))—each
with local contract
$`\Psi_{l}:{\color[rgb]{0.293,0,0.5117}noDiff}(base\_program,\cdot)`$
and a fallback that returns the original program (justified by the
reflexivity axiom). All three share
$`GMid:={\color[rgb]{0.293,0,0.5117}claude}`$ and differ only in the
prompting function $`f_{p}`$: the first generates an initial annotation
with context-specific guidance, the second repairs after a diff-checker
failure, and the third repairs after a verification failure with
error-specific feedback. The agent program
(Fig. [7](#A11.F7 "Figure 7 ‣ Appendix K Example Agents for LLM Assisted Program Verification ‣ SEVerA: Verified Self-Evolving Agents"))
dispatches to the appropriate FGGM on each loop iteration.

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Figure 4. FGGM definition for
$`{\color[rgb]{0.293,0,0.5117}initialFGGM}`$. The prompting function
builds context-specific guidance by checking for lemmas, generics, sets,
and multisets in the base program. The fallback returns the original
program, satisfying $`\Psi_{l}`$ by the reflexivity axiom.

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Figure 5. FGGM definition for
$`{\color[rgb]{0.293,0,0.5117}diffErrorFGGM}`$. Invoked when the
previous iteration’s output failed the diff checker. The prompt includes
the diff error and previous attempt, instructing the model to preserve
the base program logic.

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Figure 6. FGGM definition for
$`{\color[rgb]{0.293,0,0.5117}verifierErrorFGGM}`$. Invoked when the
previous iteration passed the diff checker but failed verification. The
prompting function analyzes the verification error to provide targeted
guidance (timeout, lemma, invariant, or type issues).

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Figure 7. Verified agent program for Dafny annotation synthesis. On the
first iteration, $`{\color[rgb]{0.293,0,0.5117}initialFGGM}`$
(Fig. [4](#A11.F4 "Figure 4 ‣ Appendix K Example Agents for LLM Assisted Program Verification ‣ SEVerA: Verified Self-Evolving Agents"))
generates an initial annotation. On subsequent iterations, the agent
dispatches to $`{\color[rgb]{0.293,0,0.5117}diffErrorFGGM}`$
(Fig. [5](#A11.F5 "Figure 5 ‣ Appendix K Example Agents for LLM Assisted Program Verification ‣ SEVerA: Verified Self-Evolving Agents"))
or $`{\color[rgb]{0.293,0,0.5117}verifierErrorFGGM}`$
(Fig. [6](#A11.F6 "Figure 6 ‣ Appendix K Example Agents for LLM Assisted Program Verification ‣ SEVerA: Verified Self-Evolving Agents"))
depending on the previous error type. Each FGGM guarantees
$`{\color[rgb]{0.293,0,0.5117}noDiff}(base\_program,y)`$, maintaining
the loop invariant. Upon exhausting all attempts, the agent returns
$`best`$, which satisfies the postcondition by the loop invariant.

## Appendix L FGGM Syntax

The syntax of a first-order guarded generative model (FGGM) can be
described using the following BNF grammar. We use the production rules
$`(\langle\text{ident}\rangle,\langle\text{type}\rangle,\langle\text{spec}\rangle,\langle\text{program}\rangle,\langle\text{string\_lit}\rangle,\langle\text{formula}\rangle)`$
from
Appendix [A](#A1 "Appendix A Restricted Dafny Grammar ‣ SEVerA: Verified Self-Evolving Agents").

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle\langle id\rangle`$ | $`\displaystyle::=\langle\text{ident}\rangle`$ |  |
|  | $`\displaystyle\langle GMid\rangle`$ | $`\displaystyle::=\langle\text{ident}\rangle`$ |  |
|  | $`\displaystyle\langle typeSig\rangle`$ | $`\displaystyle::="("\langle\text{typedVars}\rangle")""\to"\langle\text{type}\rangle`$ |  |
|  | $`\displaystyle\langle\text{typedVars}\rangle`$ | $`\displaystyle::=\langle\text{typedVar}\rangle\;\mid\;\langle\text{typedVar}\rangle,\langle\text{typedVars}\rangle`$ |  |
|  | $`\displaystyle\langle\text{typedVar}\rangle`$ | $`\displaystyle::=\langle\text{ident}\rangle:\langle\text{type}\rangle`$ |  |
|  | $`\displaystyle\langle\Phi_{l}\rangle`$ | $`\displaystyle::=\texttt{"requires"}\ \langle\text{formula}\rangle`$ |  |
|  | $`\displaystyle\langle\Psi_{l}\rangle`$ | $`\displaystyle::=\texttt{"ensures"}\ \langle\text{formula}\rangle`$ |  |
|  | $`\displaystyle\langle f_{p}{}\rangle`$ | $`\displaystyle::=\langle\text{program}\rangle`$ |  |
|  | $`\displaystyle\langle f_{d}{}\rangle`$ | $`\displaystyle::=\langle\text{program}\rangle`$ |  |
|  | $`\displaystyle\langle\text{info}\rangle`$ | $`\displaystyle::=\langle\text{string\_lit}\rangle`$ |  |

## Appendix M FGGM Validity Check

Algorithm [3](#alg3 "Algorithm 3 ‣ Appendix M FGGM Validity Check ‣ SEVerA: Verified Self-Evolving Agents")
checks whether an FGGM definition is valid. It verifies that the type
signature and local contracts are syntactically well-formed and that all
terms using library functions satisfy their input specifications. It
then checks that the prompting program and fallback program are
type-correct and terminating. Finally, the fallback program is verified
using the deductive verifier to ensure it satisfies the local contract
for all inputs. The FGGM definition is accepted only if no errors are
found.

1: Input: FGGM definition
$`\mathsf{G}{}=(id,GMid,typeSig,\Phi_{l},\Psi_{l},f_{p},f_{d})`$

2: Input: Library functions $`\mathcal{F}_{c}`$, axioms
$`\mathcal{A}{}`$

3: Output: $`\{\}`$ if valid else set of errors $`\mathsf{err}`$

4: $`\mathsf{err}\leftarrow\{\}`$

5: if $`\neg{\color[rgb]{0.293,0,0.5117}WellTyped}(typeSig)`$ then

6:
   $`\mathsf{err}\leftarrow\mathsf{err}\cup\{\text{Invalid type signature}\}`$

7: end if

8: if $`\neg{\color[rgb]{0.293,0,0.5117}WellFormedFormula}(\Phi_{l})`$
then

9:
   $`\mathsf{err}\leftarrow\mathsf{err}\cup\{\text{Invalid input contract}\}`$

10: end if

11: if $`\neg{\color[rgb]{0.293,0,0.5117}WellFormedFormula}(\Psi_{l})`$
then

12:
   $`\mathsf{err}\leftarrow\mathsf{err}\cup\{\text{Invalid output contract}\}`$

13: end if

14: if
$`\neg{\color[rgb]{0.293,0,0.5117}CheckTerms}(\Phi_{l},\mathcal{F}_{c})`$
then

15:
   $`\mathsf{err}\leftarrow\mathsf{err}\cup\{\text{Invalid library terms in }\Phi_{l}\}`$

16: end if

17: if
$`\neg{\color[rgb]{0.293,0,0.5117}CheckTerms}(\Psi_{l},\mathcal{F}_{c})`$
then

18:
   $`\mathsf{err}\leftarrow\mathsf{err}\cup\{\text{Invalid library terms in }\Psi_{l}\}`$

19: end if

20: if $`\neg{\color[rgb]{0.293,0,0.5117}TypeCheck}(f_{p})`$ or
$`\neg{\color[rgb]{0.293,0,0.5117}Terminates}(f_{p})`$ then

21:
   $`\mathsf{err}\leftarrow\mathsf{err}\cup\{\text{Invalid prompting program}\}`$

22: end if

23: if $`\neg{\color[rgb]{0.293,0,0.5117}TypeCheck}(f_{d})`$ or
$`\neg{\color[rgb]{0.293,0,0.5117}Terminates}(f_{d})`$ then

24:
   $`\mathsf{err}\leftarrow\mathsf{err}\cup\{\text{Invalid fallback program}\}`$

25: end if

26: if
$`\neg{\color[rgb]{0.293,0,0.5117}Verify}(\forall x_{1}\dots x_{n},y.\;\Phi_{l}(x_{1}\dots x_{n})\Rightarrow\Psi_{l}(x_{1}\dots x_{n},f_{d}(x_{1}\dots x_{n},y)))`$
then

27:
   $`\mathsf{err}\leftarrow\mathsf{err}\cup\{\text{Fallback violates contract}\}`$

28: end if

29: return $`\mathsf{err}`$

Algorithm 3 validateFGGM

Algorithm [4](#alg4 "Algorithm 4 ‣ Appendix M FGGM Validity Check ‣ SEVerA: Verified Self-Evolving Agents")
checks whether a concrete input–output tuple satisfies the FGGM output
contract. It first substitutes the concrete values into the
specification $`\Psi_{l}`$. If the resulting formula is quantifier-free,
the checker directly evaluates it by computing all terms using the
library functions. If the specification contains quantifiers, the
substituted formula is combined with the axioms and input specification
and submitted to an SMT solver with a timeout. The procedure returns
true only if the solver confirms satisfiability within the time bound.

1: Input: Concrete values $`(x_{1},\dots,x_{n},y)`$

2: Input: Local contracts $`(\Phi_{l},\Psi_{l})`$, axioms
$`\mathcal{A}{}`$

3: Output: $`T`$ if contract satisfied else $`F`$

4:
$`\phi\leftarrow{\color[rgb]{0.293,0,0.5117}Substitute}(\Psi_{l},\{x_{1},\dots,x_{n},y\})`$

5: if $`{\color[rgb]{0.293,0,0.5117}QuantifierFree}(\phi)`$ then

6:    if $`\phi=\neg\phi^{\prime}`$ then return
$`\neg{\color[rgb]{0.293,0,0.5117}check_{\mathcal{A},\Phi,\phi^{\prime}}}(x_{1},\dots,x_{n},y)`$

7:    else if $`\phi=\phi^{\prime}\vee\psi`$ then return
$`{\color[rgb]{0.293,0,0.5117}check_{\mathcal{A},\Phi,\phi^{\prime}}}(x_{1},\dots,x_{n},y)\vee{\color[rgb]{0.293,0,0.5117}check_{\mathcal{A},\Phi,\psi}}(x_{1},\dots,x_{n},y)`$
$`\triangleright`$ Recursively evaluate on subformulas

8:    else if $`\phi=\phi^{\prime}\wedge\psi`$ then return
$`{\color[rgb]{0.293,0,0.5117}check_{\mathcal{A},\Phi,\phi^{\prime}}}(x_{1},\dots,x_{n},y)\wedge{\color[rgb]{0.293,0,0.5117}check_{\mathcal{A},\Phi,\psi}}(x_{1},\dots,x_{n},y)`$

9:    else if $`isAtomic(\phi)`$ then return
$`\phi(x_{1},\dots,x_{n},y)`$ $`\triangleright`$ Compute the atomic
predicate $`\phi`$ value on $`(x_{1},\dots,x_{n},y)`$ $`T`$ or $`F`$

10:    end if

11: end if

12:
$`\psi\leftarrow\varphi_{\mathcal{A}{}}\wedge\Phi_{l}(x_{1},\dots,x_{n})\wedge\phi`$

13: $`res\leftarrow{\color[rgb]{0.293,0,0.5117}SMTSolve}(\psi,time)`$

14: if $`res=SAT`$ then

15:    return $`T`$

16: else

17:    return $`F`$

18: end if

## Appendix N Background on GRPO

Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO): GRPO is a reinforcement
learning–based fine-tuning method for generative models that optimizes a
policy by comparing outputs *relative to other samples from the same
input*, rather than relying on an explicit value function. Let
$`\pi_{\theta}(y\mid p)`$ denote the parametric policy for an FGGM
$`{\color[rgb]{0.293,0,0.5117}id_{\theta_{i}}}`$, where
$`p\in\mathbb{P}`$ is the input prompt and
$`y_{l}\sim\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid p)`$ is a sampled output. For each
input $`p`$, GRPO samples a *group* of $`G`$ candidate outputs
$`\{y^{(1)},\dots,y^{(G)}\}`$ from the current policy. Each sample is
assigned a scalar reward $`r^{(j)}=\mathcal{R}(p,y^{(j)})`$. Instead of
using absolute rewards directly, GRPO computes *relative advantages*
within the group:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
| (24) |  | $`\displaystyle A^{(j)}=\frac{r^{(j)}-\mu_{p}}{\sigma_{p}},\hskip 9.24994pt\mu_{p}=\tfrac{1}{G}\sum_{j=1}^{G}r^{(j)},\hskip 9.24994pt\sigma_{p}=\sqrt{\tfrac{1}{G}\sum_{j=1}^{G}(r^{(j)}-\mu_{p})^{2}+\epsilon}`$ |  |

Here $`\mu_{p}`$ and $`\sigma_{p}`$ are the mean and standard deviation
of rewards within the group.

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
| (25) |  | $`\displaystyle\max_{\theta}\;\;\mathbb{E}_{p\sim\mathbb{P}}\left[\tfrac{1}{G}\sum_{j=1}^{G}\min\Big(\rho^{(j)}A^{(j)},\;\text{clip}(\rho^{(j)},1-\epsilon,1+\epsilon)A^{(j)}\Big)\right]`$ |  |

where
$`\rho^{(j)}=\frac{\pi_{\theta}(y^{(j)}\mid p)}{\pi_{\theta_{\text{old}}}(y^{(j)}\mid p)}`$
is the importance ratio. This clipped objective, similar to PPO, ensures
stable policy updates. In our setting, each FGGM
$`{\color[rgb]{0.293,0,0.5117}id_{\theta_{i}}}`$ defines a policy
$`\pi_{\theta_{i}}(y_{l}\mid p)`$ over outputs $`y_{l}`$ for input
$`p`$. The reward function defined in
Eq. [23](#S5.E23 "In 5.2.5. Learn ‣ 5.2. Key Steps ‣ 5. Technical Details ‣ SEVerA: Verified Self-Evolving Agents"):

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
| (26) |  | $`\displaystyle\mathcal{R}(p,y_{l})=1-{\color[rgb]{0.293,0,0.5117}Sigmoid}\big(\mathsf{L}{}(x,\_,y)\times\mathbb{I}(y=y_{l})+\lambda\times(1-\mathbb{I}({\color[rgb]{0.293,0,0.5117}check_{\mathcal{A},\Phi_{l},\Psi_{l}}}(p,y_{l})))\big)`$ |  |

## Appendix P Planner Feedback

After each search–verify–learn iteration, SEVerA constructs structured
feedback $`I^{\prime}`$ from the execution traces of the current best
candidate agent on the training data $`\mathrm{D}`$
(Algorithm [2](#alg2 "Algorithm 2 ‣ 5.2.6. SEVerA ‣ 5.2. Key Steps ‣ 5. Technical Details ‣ SEVerA: Verified Self-Evolving Agents"),
line 31). The planner LLM receives the task-performance score of the
previous program along with per-example error diagnostics. Specifically,
for each training example on which the previous candidate failed, SEVerA
provides the planner with the example input, the agent’s output, and the
corresponding error message (e.g., a verification error, a grammar
violation, or an incorrect answer). The planner is then asked to
generate a one-to-two sentence description and a suggested fix for each
failed example. The resulting list of per-example descriptions and
suggestions is collected and fed back to the planner as part of the
context $`I^{\prime}`$ when it samples the next candidate program. This
feedback mechanism enables the planner to identify recurring failure
patterns and adjust its synthesized FGGM definitions and prompting
programs $`f_{p}`$ accordingly in subsequent iterations.

## Appendix R Proof Details

See
[5.1](#S5.Thmtheorem1 "Lemma 5.1 (Completeness of Checker). ‣ 5.2.2. FGGM Well-formedness ‣ 5.2. Key Steps ‣ 5. Technical Details ‣ SEVerA: Verified Self-Evolving Agents")

###### Proof of Lemma [5.1](#S5.Thmtheorem1 "Lemma 5.1 (Completeness of Checker). ‣ 5.2.2. FGGM Well-formedness ‣ 5.2. Key Steps ‣ 5. Technical Details ‣ SEVerA: Verified Self-Evolving Agents").

We prove the claim by structural induction on the quantifier-free
formula $`\Psi_{l}`$. Fix arbitrary $`(x_{1},\dots,x_{n},y)`$. We show:

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
{\color[rgb]{0.293,0,0.5117}check_{\mathcal{A},\Phi_{l},\Psi_{l}}}(x_{1},\dots,x_{n},y)\iff\Psi_{l}(x_{1},\dots,x_{n},y).
``` |  |

##### Base case.

Suppose $`\Psi_{l}`$ is an atomic predicate $`P(x_{1},\dots,x_{n},y)`$
over terms constructed from computable library functions in
$`\mathcal{F}_{c}`$. Under the substitution $`(x_{1},\dots,x_{n},y)`$,
$`{\color[rgb]{0.293,0,0.5117}check_{\mathcal{A},\Phi,P}}`$ evaluates
each term by executing the corresponding functions in
$`\mathcal{F}_{c}`$. Since these functions are computable
$`{\color[rgb]{0.293,0,0.5117}check_{\mathcal{A},\Phi,P}}`$ exactly
computes the atomic predicate $`P(x_{1},\dots,x_{n},y)`$ on
$`(x_{1},\dots,x_{n},y)`$ which reduces to $`T`$ or $`F`$.

##### Inductive step.

Assume the claim holds for formulas $`\phi`$ and $`\psi`$ i.e.
$`{\color[rgb]{0.293,0,0.5117}check_{\mathcal{A},\Phi,\phi}}(x_{1},\dots,x_{n},y)\iff\phi(x_{1},\dots,x_{n},y)`$
and
$`{\color[rgb]{0.293,0,0.5117}check_{\mathcal{A},\Phi,\psi}}(x_{1},\dots,x_{n},y)\iff\psi(x_{1},\dots,x_{n},y)`$
We show it holds for compound formulas:

- •
  If $`\Psi_{l}=\neg\phi`$, then by definition of
  $`{\color[rgb]{0.293,0,0.5117}check_{\mathcal{A},\Phi_{l},\Psi_{l}}}`$,

  |  |  |  |
  |----|----|----|
  |  |
  ``` math
  {\color[rgb]{0.293,0,0.5117}check_{\mathcal{A},\Phi_{l},\Psi_{l}}}(x_{1},\dots,x_{n},y)=\neg{\color[rgb]{0.293,0,0.5117}check_{\mathcal{A},\Phi,\phi}}(x_{1},\dots,x_{n},y).
  ``` |  |

  By the inductive hypothesis,

  |  |  |  |
  |----|----|----|
  |  | $`\displaystyle{\color[rgb]{0.293,0,0.5117}check_{\mathcal{A},\Phi_{l},\Psi_{l}}}(x_{1},\dots,x_{n},y)\iff\neg\big({\color[rgb]{0.293,0,0.5117}check_{\mathcal{A},\Phi,\phi}}(x_{1},\dots,x_{n},y)\big)\iff`$ |  |
  |  | $`\displaystyle\neg\big(\phi(x_{1},\dots,x_{n},y)\big)\iff\Psi_{l}(x_{1},\dots,x_{n},y)`$ |  |
- •
  If $`\Psi_{l}=\phi\wedge\psi`$, then

  |  |  |  |
  |----|----|----|
  |  |
  ``` math
  {\color[rgb]{0.293,0,0.5117}check_{\mathcal{A},\Phi_{l},\Psi_{l}}}(x_{1},\dots,x_{n},y)={\color[rgb]{0.293,0,0.5117}check_{\mathcal{A},\Phi,\phi}}(x_{1},\dots,x_{n},y)\wedge{\color[rgb]{0.293,0,0.5117}check_{\mathcal{A},\Phi,\psi}}(x_{1},\dots,x_{n},y),
  ``` |  |

  which, by the inductive hypothesis,

  |  |  |  |
  |----|----|----|
  |  | $`\displaystyle{\color[rgb]{0.293,0,0.5117}check_{\mathcal{A},\Phi_{l},\Psi_{l}}}(x_{1},\dots,x_{n},y)\iff\big({\color[rgb]{0.293,0,0.5117}check_{\mathcal{A},\Phi,\phi}}(x_{1},\dots,x_{n},y)\wedge{\color[rgb]{0.293,0,0.5117}check_{\mathcal{A},\Phi,\psi}}(x_{1},\dots,x_{n},y)\big)`$ |  |
  |  | $`\displaystyle\iff\big(\phi(x_{1},\dots,x_{n},y)\wedge\psi(x_{1},\dots,x_{n},y)\big)\iff\Psi_{l}(x_{1},\dots,x_{n},y)`$ |  |
- •
  If $`\Psi_{l}=\phi\vee\psi`$, the argument is analogous tp
  $`\Psi_{l}=\phi\wedge\psi`$.

∎

###### Lemma R.1 (Checker Soundness).

$`\varphi_{\mathcal{A}{}}\implies\big(\forall x_{1}\in T_{1},\dots,\forall x_{n}\in T_{n},\forall y\in T_{o}.\;\Phi_{l}(x_{1},\dots,x_{n})\implies\left({\color[rgb]{0.293,0,0.5117}check_{\mathcal{A},\Phi_{l},\Psi_{l}}}(x_{1},\dots,x_{n},y)\implies\Psi_{l}(x_{1},\dots,x_{n},y)\right)\big)`$.

###### Proof.

For quantifier-free $`\Psi_{l}`$ soundness follows from
Lemma [5.1](#S5.Thmtheorem1 "Lemma 5.1 (Completeness of Checker). ‣ 5.2.2. FGGM Well-formedness ‣ 5.2. Key Steps ‣ 5. Technical Details ‣ SEVerA: Verified Self-Evolving Agents").
For $`\Psi_{l}`$ with qunatifier
$`{\color[rgb]{0.293,0,0.5117}check_{\mathcal{A},\Phi_{l},\Psi_{l}}}{}`$
returns true if
$`(\varphi_{\mathcal{A}{}}\wedge\Phi_{l}(x_{1},\dots,x_{n}))\wedge\Psi_{l}(x_{1},\dots,x_{n},y)`$
is evalautes to true within timeout. Hence for any
$`(x_{1},\dots,x_{n},y)`$

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle{\color[rgb]{0.293,0,0.5117}check_{\mathcal{A},\Phi_{l},\Psi_{l}}}{}(x_{1},\dots,x_{n},y)\implies(\varphi_{\mathcal{A}{}}\wedge\Phi_{l}(x_{1},\dots,x_{n}))\wedge\Psi_{l}(x_{1},\dots,x_{n},y)`$ |  |  |
|  | $`\displaystyle(\varphi_{\mathcal{A}{}}\wedge{\color[rgb]{0.293,0,0.5117}check_{\mathcal{A},\Phi_{l},\Psi_{l}}}{}(x_{1},\dots,x_{n},y))\implies\Phi_{l}(x_{1},\dots,x_{n})\wedge\Psi_{l}(x_{1},\dots,x_{n},y)`$ |  |  |
|  | $`\displaystyle(\varphi_{\mathcal{A}{}}\wedge{\color[rgb]{0.293,0,0.5117}check_{\mathcal{A},\Phi_{l},\Psi_{l}}}{}(x_{1},\dots,x_{n},y)\wedge\Phi_{l}(x_{1},\dots,x_{n}))\implies\Psi_{l}(x_{1},\dots,x_{n},y)`$ |  |  |
|  | $`\displaystyle(\varphi_{\mathcal{A}{}}\wedge\Phi_{l}(x_{1},\dots,x_{n}))\implies({\color[rgb]{0.293,0,0.5117}check_{\mathcal{A},\Phi_{l},\Psi_{l}}}{}(x_{1},\dots,x_{n},y))\implies\Psi_{l}(x_{1},\dots,x_{n},y))`$ |  |  |
| (27) |  | $`\displaystyle\varphi_{\mathcal{A}{}}\implies\big(\Phi_{l}(x_{1},\dots,x_{n}))\implies(({\color[rgb]{0.293,0,0.5117}check_{\mathcal{A},\Phi_{l},\Psi_{l}}}{}(x_{1},\dots,x_{n},y))\implies\Psi_{l}(x_{1},\dots,x_{n},y))\big)`$ |  |

From
Eq [27](#A18.E27 "In Proof. ‣ Inductive step. ‣ Appendix R Proof Details ‣ SEVerA: Verified Self-Evolving Agents")
it follows ,
$`\varphi_{\mathcal{A}{}}\implies\big(\forall x_{1}\in T_{1},\dots,\forall x_{n}\in T_{n},\forall y\in T_{o}.\;\Phi_{l}(x_{1},\dots,x_{n})\implies\left({\color[rgb]{0.293,0,0.5117}check_{\mathcal{A},\Phi_{l},\Psi_{l}}}(x_{1},\dots,x_{n},y)\implies\Psi_{l}(x_{1},\dots,x_{n},y)\right)\big)`$.
∎

See
[5.2](#S5.Thmtheorem2 "Theorem 5.2 (Valid Local contract). ‣ 5.2.2. FGGM Well-formedness ‣ 5.2. Key Steps ‣ 5. Technical Details ‣ SEVerA: Verified Self-Evolving Agents")

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle\forall x_{1}\in T_{1},\dots,\forall x_{n}\in T_{n},\;\Phi(x_{1},\dots,x_{n})\implies\Psi(x_{1},\dots,x_{n},f(x_{1},\dots,x_{n})).`$ |  |

∎

See
[5.5](#S5.Thmtheorem5 "Theorem 5.5 (Sufficient Success Condition). ‣ 5.3. Theoretical Results ‣ 5. Technical Details ‣ SEVerA: Verified Self-Evolving Agents")

###### Proof.

Let $`f_{n}^{\theta}:T_{1}\times\cdots\times T_{n}\to T_{o}`$ be any
type-correct generative model. By assumption (iii), there exists
$`f_{d}\in\mathsf{S}(G,\mathcal{F}_{c})`$ such that

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\varphi_{\mathcal{A}{}}\implies\forall x_{1},\dots,x_{n}.;\Phi(x_{1},\dots,x_{n})\implies\Psi(x_{1},\dots,x_{n},f_{d}(x_{1},\dots,x_{n})).
``` |  |

Construction. Define

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\mathsf{G}{}=({\color[rgb]{0.293,0,0.5117}id},f_{n}^{\theta},\tau,\Phi_{l},\Psi_{l},f_{p},f_{d},info),
``` |  |

with $`(\Phi_{l},\Psi_{l}):=(\Phi,\Psi)`$ and any well-typed $`f_{p}`$.
Since $`f_{d}`$ satisfies the contract and $`\Psi`$ is quantifier-free,
$`\mathsf{G}{}`$ is valid and
$`{\color[rgb]{0.293,0,0.5117}check_{\mathcal{A},\Phi_{l},\Psi_{l}}}`$
is complete
(Lemma [5.1](#S5.Thmtheorem1 "Lemma 5.1 (Completeness of Checker). ‣ 5.2.2. FGGM Well-formedness ‣ 5.2. Key Steps ‣ 5. Technical Details ‣ SEVerA: Verified Self-Evolving Agents")).

Define the program $`f\in\mathsf{S}(G,\mathcal{F})`$ as:

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
{\color[rgb]{0,0.3594,0.668}\textbf{function}}\ {\color[rgb]{0.293,0,0.5117}f}(x_{1}:T_{1},\dots,x_{n}:T_{n}):T_{o}\ {\{{\color[rgb]{0,0.3594,0.668}\textbf{return}}\ {\color[rgb]{0.293,0,0.5117}id}(x_{1},\dots,x_{n});\}}.
``` |  |

Correctness. For any $`(x_{1},\dots,x_{n})`$ such that
$`\Phi(x_{1},\dots,x_{n})`$ holds, by
Theorem [5.2](#S5.Thmtheorem2 "Theorem 5.2 (Valid Local contract). ‣ 5.2.2. FGGM Well-formedness ‣ 5.2. Key Steps ‣ 5. Technical Details ‣ SEVerA: Verified Self-Evolving Agents"),

|     |                                               |     |
|-----|-----------------------------------------------|-----|
|     |
       ``` math
       \Psi(x_{1},\dots,x_{n},f(x_{1},\dots,x_{n})).
       ```                                            |     |

Output of $`f`$. Fix $`(x_{1},\dots,x_{n})`$ with
$`\Phi(x_{1},\dots,x_{n})`$. By completeness,

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
{\color[rgb]{0.293,0,0.5117}check_{\mathcal{A},\Phi_{l},\Psi_{l}}}(x_{1},\dots,x_{n},y)\iff\Psi(x_{1},\dots,x_{n},y).
``` |  |

Hence,

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
f(x_{1},\dots,x_{n})=\begin{cases}f_{n}^{\theta}(x_{1},\dots,x_{n})&\text{if }\Psi(x_{1},\dots,x_{n},f_{n}^{\theta}(x_{1},\dots,x_{n})),\\
f_{d}(x_{1},\dots,x_{n})&\text{otherwise.}\end{cases}
``` |  |

Loss comparison. For any $`(x,\_)\in\mathrm{D}`$:

*Case 1:* $`\Psi(x,f_{n}^{\theta}(x))`$. Then $`f(x)=f_{n}^{\theta}(x)`$
and

|     |                                                               |     |
|-----|---------------------------------------------------------------|-----|
|     |
       ``` math
       \mathsf{L}{}(x,\_,f(x))=\mathsf{L}{}(x,\_,f_{n}^{\theta}(x)).
       ```                                                            |     |

*Case 2:* $`\neg\Psi(x,f_{n}^{\theta}(x))`$. Then $`f(x)=f_{d}(x)`$ and
$`\Psi(x,f(x))`$ holds. By assumption (i),

|     |                                                               |     |
|-----|---------------------------------------------------------------|-----|
|     |
       ``` math
       \mathsf{L}{}(x,\_,f(x))<\mathsf{L}{}(x,\_,f_{n}^{\theta}(x)).
       ```                                                            |     |

Thus,

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\forall(x,\_)\in\mathrm{D}.\quad\mathsf{L}{}(x,\_,f(x))\leq\mathsf{L}{}(x,\_,f_{n}^{\theta}(x)),
``` |  |

which implies

|     |                                                  |     |
|-----|--------------------------------------------------|-----|
|     |
       ``` math
       \mathsf{L}{}(f)\leq\mathsf{L}{}(f_{n}^{\theta}).
       ```                                               |     |

Strict improvement. If $`\exists(x,_{)}\in\mathrm{D}`$ such that
$`\neg\Psi(x,f_{n}^{\theta}(x))`$, then Case 2 holds for at least one
point, yielding

|     |                                               |     |
|-----|-----------------------------------------------|-----|
|     |
       ``` math
       \mathsf{L}{}(f)<\mathsf{L}{}(f_{n}^{\theta}).
       ```                                            |     |

Conclusion. The constructed program $`f`$ satisfies $`(\Phi,\Psi)`$ and
achieves no greater loss than $`f_{n}^{\theta}`$, with strict
improvement when violations occur. Note the program verification setup
satisfies this sufficient condition. ∎
````
